articles.title: Syria mulls military aid to Saudi Arabia as Houthis escalate war
articles.summary: Syria is weighing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia, U.S. and Syrian officials said, as the Iran-aligned Houthis step up missile and drone attacks on the kingdom that ki...
articles.full_text:
Syria is weighing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia, U.S. and Syrian officials said, as the Iran-aligned Houthis step up missile and drone attacks on the kingdom that killed three people at Saudi airports this week.
The possible entry of Syrian forces into the battle, a spillover of the US-Iran conflict, shows how Yemen's reignited civil war has added new chaos to a region already aflame and risks drawing regional states into grueling mountain fighting.
Saudi Arabia has pushed for support from allied nations, including Türkiye and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or purely defensive capacity, an effort made more urgent by the Houthi strikes on its infrastructure such as this week's deadly airport attacks.
A succession of loud booms were reported in Riyadh Thursday morning. There was no immediate official comment and no public early warning alerts, although some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh warned parents of shelter in place orders, according to Reuters.
Yemen's Houthi rebels, however, claimed Thursday that it had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
One person had been killed in a strike on Riyadh airport and two others in an attack on Abha airport in the southwest Tuesday and Wednesday, Saudi Arabia said late Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the U.S. and Syrian officials said Damascus was carefully considering military support, including the option of defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks or deployment in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops take the fight to the Houthis.
Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a cease-fire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis have said they were responding to attacks from the Saudi-backed government, which the government denies.
The group's threats to shipping along a waterway that has become ever more critical for Gulf oil exports since Iran's attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and its targeting of Saudi cities and infrastructure, have drawn the kingdom back in.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian Foreign Ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's 14-year civil war.
"Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries," the diplomat said in a statement.
This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a counterattack, taking back areas around the strait as they push to reverse the Houthis' gains of last month.
However, in a messy war with several frontlines, the Houthis have also made some gains of their own this week, surrounding the country's third-largest city of Taiz by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden.
The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of Saudi-backed forces under the internationally recognized government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed.
Saudi Arabia this summer agreed the Mecca pact with Türkiye and Pakistan, committing all three countries to come to each other's defense, though Ankara still needs to ratify the treaty internally.
NATO-member Türkiye said Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis, and a Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.
Pakistan, meanwhile, has flown cargo planes of military equipment to Aden in southern Yemen to help in the battle against the Houthis, sources in Pakistan have said and has deployed troops inside Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom's borders.

articles.title: Plane damage reported as Houthis target Riyadh airport again
articles.summary: Several explosions were heard in Saudi Arabia's capital on Thursday, including a large blast at Riyadh’s international airport, according to reports, a day after the kingdom said a...
articles.full_text:
Several explosions were heard in Saudi Arabia's capital on Thursday, including a large blast at Riyadh’s international airport, according to reports, a day after the kingdom said an attack on the civil aviation hub killed one person and wounded others.
The blasts had an immediate effect on markets, as the price of crude oil jumped and Saudi Arabia slid further into the latest front in the Iran war. Hundreds of flights to and from Riyadh were cancelled, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen claimed responsibility for the new attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, saying the ballistic missile caused damage but giving no evidence. The Saudis had no immediate comment about the claim.
One source briefed on the matter told Agence France-Presse (AFP) at least one plane had suffered catastrophic damage at the transit hub, while a second said three aircraft were hit.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the rebels, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said they intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh, along with a ballistic missile fired toward Khamis Mushait, in the southwest near the Yemen border.
Saudi civil defense authorities said debris from an interception damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex, with no mention of any casualties.
The Houthis have repeatedly claimed attacks against Saudi airports, military and oil facilities in recent days.
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesperson, said in a statement late Thursday that the rebels fired more ballistic and cruise missiles at the airports in Riyadh and the southwestern city of Najran, near the border with Yemen, disrupting flights.
Earlier, the rebels had warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace.
In their new statement, the Houthis also warned people in Saudi Arabia to stay away from oil facilities that "represent targets for our forces" as the rebels press a declared blockade against the world's top oil exporter.
King Khalid International Airport "closed again," the Flightradar24 monitor said Thursday afternoon on the social media platform X not long after the blasts. "Last landing 80+ minutes ago. Last take off 90+ minutes ago."
Fire and ambulance crews were deployed and smoke was visible, the Associated Press (AP) said, citing a witness.
The witness said outgoing flights were halted and passengers were instructed to leave checked-in luggage behind and evacuate.
The Indian Embassy in Riyadh said on X that Air India has suspended operations through Saturday, while Lufthansa Group said in a statement that its airlines will suspend their flights to Riyadh through Oct. 16.
A U.S. Embassy security alert issued Wednesday said citizens should be aware of potential airspace closures and told U.S. government employees not to travel within 32 kilometers (20 miles) of the Yemen border.
On Wednesday, Saudi officials said attacks on the Riyadh and Abha airports claimed by the Houthis had killed three people – the first deaths since Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces launched a major ground and air offensive against the rebels.
The offensive is aimed at retaking territory that the Houthis seized a month ago along Yemen's western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The rebels' presence on the Bab el-Mandeb poses a threat to the crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic has been curtailed due to Iran's attacks on ships.
Rebel leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi on Thursday accused Saudi Arabia of turning the area around the Bab el-Mandeb into a war zone.
The deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia brought condemnation from countries including Britain, India, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and others.
Also Wednesday, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said forces destroyed a platform in Yemen's rebel-held capital of Sanaa that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital.
Saudi Arabia has sought support from allies, including the United States, in the face of the Houthi attacks. Officials have said U.S. support has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive.
Türkiye and Pakistan are assessing possible air defense, electronic warfare and technical assistance for Saudi Arabia under a trilateral agreement, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said, while stressing that the deal is defensive, not offensive.
"Türkiye will not be sending troops into another country's territory to carry out an attack," he said, adding that Ankara was trying to resolve the issue through diplomacy.
Pakistan's Information Ministry on Thursday said relevant authorities would provide details of any military involvement if necessary.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia says 3 injured in renewed Houthi attacks - The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia says 3 injured in renewed Houthi attacks  The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia said three people were injured in the latest attacks on its airports since fighting with Yemen's Houthi rebels reignited. Meanwhile, Palestinian officials said Israeli airstrikes in Gaza City killed two people, while condemning home demolitions in east Jerusalem and violence in the occupied West Bank.
Israelis are readying to mark the third anniversary of the Palestinian militant Hamas group's Oct. 7, 2023, attack as conflict in the Middle East has spread to include Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen.
Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said airports in the cities of Najran and Jizan were hit Monday, damaging both facilities and leaving three lightly injured. The statement didn't say who was responsible, but followed an announcement by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels that they fired missiles and drones at the kingdom.
Houthi Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said in a statement that they had fired toward a third airport on Tuesday. The Associated Press could not confirm whether the Houthis had hit Abha International Airport. Saudi authorities did not immediately comment.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said Tuesday it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Khamis Mushait, a city in southwestern Saudi Arabia that's home to a major Saudi military base.
The Houthis were fighting Tuesday around Dhubab, a strategic town in Yemen that its internationally recognized government had previously said it had retaken, a senior Yemeni military official told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters.
Saudi Arabia and its allies in Yemen's government have launched a military campaign to reclaim Houthi-controlled territory near the southern tip of the Red Sea to prevent disruptions to oil being exported out of the region.
An outbound tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an "unknown projectile" on Monday, the British military said in a late report Tuesday. There were no immediate reports of casualties or environmental impact.
Even as Iran has lost its near-complete chokehold on the strait, the ongoing risk of Iranian attacks keeps overall ship traffic well below prewar levels.
2 KILLED IN GAZA
Two Israeli airstrikes killed two people in Gaza City, health officials at the city's Shifa Hospital said. Israel's military said it targeted militants in both strikes.
It was the latest deadly attack since a ceasefire nearly a year ago in the Israel-Hamas war triggered by the 2023 attack, when Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people, most civilians, in southern Israel and abducted 251 others. More than 1,460 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at a Cabinet meeting on Tuesday that Hamas could attack Israel in a bid to influence the outcome of the country's elections later this month. Netanyahu, who is locked in a tough battle for reelection, did not publicly provide evidence for the claim.
In recent days, Netanyahu's political opponents have pointed to the thwarted FlyDubai cockpit attack as the latest example of his government's failure to manage security threats.
Jaafar Ashtiyeh, a veteran Palestinian photojournalist for Agence France-Presse, said he was filming the olive harvest in the West Bank village of Aqraba when he heard shooting by Israeli settlers. He said they later encircled him, took his camera as he was filming the attack and beat him, causing injuries that required hospitalization.
The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel, Gaza and the West Bank, urged Israel to "investigate why soldiers present in the area did not intervene in this attack against clearly identified journalists."
The Palestinian Authority said settlers in the area also shot one man in the leg and severely beat two others in the town south of Nablus. Israel's military did not provide immediate comment.
Israeli authorities tore down a five-story building in east Jerusalem on Tuesday.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir attended the demolition and said Israeli authorities had demolished more than 10,000 structures built without permits over the past year and a half.
Palestinians say procuring construction permits is nearly impossible for them in east Jerusalem, which Israel annexed in the 1967 Mideast war and is home to almost 400,000 Palestinians.
Information for this article was contributed by Ahmed al Haj of The Associated Press.

articles.title: Iran's atomic energy chief asserts nuclear industry resilience despite sanctions - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: Iran's atomic energy chief asserts nuclear industry resilience despite sanctions  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Iranian Vice President and Head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI), Mohammad Eslami, has issued a staunch defense of his country's nuclear program, declaring that Tehran has not halted its nuclear industry activities despite years of crippling international sanctions and alleged acts of sabotage. Speaking in October 2026, Eslami emphasized that the fundamental basis of Iran's nuclear strategy remains enrichment, asserting that no foreign power possesses the legal or practical authority to deprive the nation of its rights under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) to develop peaceful nuclear technology.
Eslami's remarks come at a time of heightened geopolitical tension and diplomatic stalemate regarding Iran's nuclear capabilities. Western powers and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) have repeatedly expressed concern over Tehran's accumulation of highly enriched uranium and its increasing restrictions on inspector access. However, the AEOI chief framed these challenges as temporary obstacles that have ultimately failed to derail the country's long-term scientific and industrial objectives. He highlighted that the nuclear industry continues to advance, pointing to the development of advanced centrifuges and the expansion of nuclear applications in medicine, agriculture, and domestic energy production as evidence of the program's resilience.
The Iranian official also touched upon the history of alleged sabotage and targeted attacks against Iranian nuclear scientists and facilities, suggesting that such actions by hostile entities have only served to galvanize domestic resolve and accelerate indigenous technological development. By portraying the nuclear program as a matter of national sovereignty and scientific pride, Eslami is reinforcing the government's narrative that external pressure is counterproductive. This stance is particularly significant for domestic consumption, as the administration seeks to project strength and self-reliance to a populace weary of economic hardships exacerbated by sanctions.
From a technical perspective, Iran's nuclear infrastructure has undergone significant transformations since the collapse of the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA). The country has installed thousands of advanced IR-6 and IR-4 centrifuges at its Natanz and Fordow facilities, significantly reducing the time required to produce fissile material. Eslami's insistence that activities have not halted serves as a signal to international negotiators that Tehran retains the leverage and technical capacity to dictate the terms of any future diplomatic engagement, rather than being forced into concessions by economic duress.
The international community remains divided on how to respond to Iran's nuclear posture. While the United States and European allies continue to advocate for a return to verifiable limits on enrichment, regional actors in the Middle East view Iran's advancing capabilities as a direct security threat. Eslami's comments underscore the difficulty of finding a mutually acceptable framework that addresses Western proliferation concerns while accommodating Iran's demands for sanctions relief and recognition of its technological achievements. The AEOI continues to operate under a complex web of IAEA safeguards, though the level of transparency has fluctuated with the political climate.
Looking ahead, the trajectory of Iran's nuclear industry will likely remain a central flashpoint in global security debates. Eslami's assertion of uninterrupted progress indicates that Tehran is prepared to maintain its current course, leveraging its nuclear advancements as a strategic asset in broader negotiations over regional influence and economic integration. For the international community, the challenge remains to balance the enforcement of non-proliferation norms with the reality of a nuclear threshold state that has demonstrated a remarkable capacity to adapt to and circumvent external pressures.

articles.summary: King David Hotel bombing to consulate row: A timeline of UK-Israel tension  Al JazeeraIsrael Downgrades U.K. Consulate in Jerusalem Over West Bank Trade Ban  WSJBritish diplomats to remain at scaled-down mission in Jerusalem  ReutersIsrael and U.K. Cut Last-Minute Deal to Avoid Full Closure of British Consulate in East Jerusalem  The New York TimesIsrael’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on Jerusalem  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
The British Consulate General in occupied East Jerusalem has ceased operating under that name after Israel ordered it to close in retaliation for the United Kingdom’s sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
However, UK officials insisted on Thursday that it remains open, albeit under its new title of “UK Mission”.
This isn’t the first time tensions have arisen between Israel and the UK, however. Here’s more about the times relations have faltered.
Why did Israel order the British consulate to close?
Last month, Israel gave the UK 30 days to close the consulate, after which it said British diplomats working there would lose their diplomatic status.
The order came a day after Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the UK would ban imports of all goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank and would bar companies from providing them with services, including financing, construction and real estate.
As the deadline expired, the two governments reached a last-minute compromise, however.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said Israel would allow a team of seven British diplomats to work from the building, while 20 diplomats, including the consul general, would leave Israel. The name of the building has also been changed.
Miliband said the building would not close and would now be called the “UK Mission, Jerusalem”, and insisted that the UK does not accept that Israel has the legal right to close a consulate, which the UK owns and which has stood for nearly 200 years.
Besides assisting UK nationals in Palestine, the mission provides support to Palestinians and generally represents the UK in East Jerusalem, the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
Britain and Israel have mostly enjoyed strong and warm relations. But Israel’s move against the consulate is not the first time there has been tension between them.
Here is a timeline of some of those moments of strain:
The King David Hotel bombing
Britain’s role in the founding of Israel dates back to a single letter. On November 2, 1917, Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour wrote to Lord Rothschild that the British government viewed the establishment of a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine “with favour”, provided nothing was done to prejudice the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities.
Britain went on to rule Palestine under a League of Nations mandate. By the 1940s, Zionist armed groups had turned their guns on the British administration itself.
The deadliest attack came on July 22, 1946. Members of the Irgun, a Zionist underground group, disguised themselves as hotel staff and carried about 350kg of explosives into the basement of the King David Hotel in Jerusalem. The hotel housed the Secretariat of the Government of Palestine and the headquarters of British forces in Palestine and Transjordan.
Menachem Begin, then head of the Irgun, ordered the bombing. The blast killed 91 people: 41 Arabs, 28 Britons, 17 Jews and five others. Begin later became Israel’s prime minister.
The Irgun claimed it had called in three warnings ahead of the explosion by telephone to the hotel switchboard, the French Consulate and the Palestine Post, giving occupants time to evacuate.
The British authorities did not deny that warnings were sent, but maintained that none reached anyone “in an official position with any power to take action”. The exact sequence of events remains contested: some accounts claim the hotel warning was ignored entirely, while others suggest hotel management did not take the threat seriously. What is not disputed is that the building was not evacuated in time.
The Irgun also claimed that a senior British official, Sir John Shaw, refused to act on its warning, which he strenuously denied.
Close to war during Israel’s formation
Britain withdrew from Palestine in May 1948, and Israel declared itself an independent state. Amid the war that followed with neighbouring Arab states, British and Israeli forces came close to direct confrontation.
In late December 1948, Israeli forces pushed into Egyptian territory in Sinai. A United States Department of State message to its ambassador in Tel Aviv warned that unless Israeli forces withdrew, Britain would be bound to fulfil its obligations under its 1936 treaty with Egypt, so Israel pulled back.
Days later, however, the two sides clashed in the air. On January 7, 1949, Israeli forces shot down four Royal Air Force Spitfires, and a Hawker Tempest later that day. The precise location is unclear, but some sources place it near the Deir el-Balah area of what is now the Gaza Strip, but was then about 25km (15 miles) inside Egyptian territory. Two British pilots were killed, including the Tempest’s pilot, David Tattersfield. Israel said its pilots had mistaken the British aircraft for Egyptian ones.
On January 8, the UK announced it was sending forces to Aqaba, on modern-day Jordan’s Red Sea coast, at Transjordan’s request. In his diary, David Ben-Gurion wrote that he had consulted his top commanders on how to deal with the threat of British intervention. Washington helped calm things down: President Harry Truman criticised the British handling of the crisis.
Historians still debate how close the two sides came to war. Some argue the UK worked to avoid confrontation and never issued a formal ultimatum. Either way, Britain withheld de jure recognition of Israel until April 1950.
UK weapons embargo over invasion of Lebanon
When Israel invaded Lebanon in June 1982, the UK took action. Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher later wrote that Britain restricted defence sales to Israel in June 1982 in direct response to the invasion. The embargo lasted until 1994.
Foreign Secretary Francis Pym publicly condemned the invasion, and government papers declassified years later show London was furious in private as well. The UK even refused to send Israel gas masks during the 1991 Gulf War, when Iraqi missiles struck Tel Aviv.
Falklands tensions
The same year – 1982 – the UK went to war with Argentina over the Falkland Islands, and Israel sent arms to the other side.
According to declassified British files, Israel sold Argentina weapons including Skyhawk jets, which killed dozens of British troops. Foreign Secretary Geoffrey Howe personally asked Israel to stop, but his request was ignored. Israeli arms were also routed through Peru so that the UK would not find out.
Israel denied involvement at first but, by 1984, admitted to supplying Argentina in order to sustain its arms industry. British officials suspected another motive, however. They believed Begin, by then prime minister, still bore a grudge against the UK from the Mandate era.
Gaza genocide: The current crisis
Relations between the UK and Israel have also dipped since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023. More than 74,000 people in Gaza have been killed in Israeli strikes and its siege of the strip, including about 1,400 of those since a supposed US-led “ceasefire” was declared one year ago. Most of the dead are women and children. Thousands more are lost under the rubble and presumed dead.
In September 2024, the UK suspended 30 arms export licences to Israel. In May 2025, it suspended trade talks and sanctioned individuals and companies linked to settler violence. In September 2025, it formally recognised the State of Palestine.
Last September, London went further. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who is himself Jewish, said the UK now regards Israel’s occupation of the West Bank, not just the illegal settlements there, as illegal. He told parliament that Palestinians are being ethnically cleansed by settlers in parts of the West Bank.
Israel’s response was swift. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said he had urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to close the consulate, accusing it of working on behalf of the Palestinian Authority. Israeli Foreign Minister Saar blamed London: “We did not want it to come to this, but the Labour Government’s actions have led us here.”
The compromise has eased the immediate standoff without resolving it. Saar said the UK had agreed not to retaliate, while Miliband said it would hold off on reciprocal action as long as talks remain credible.
“What’s happening here is that Israel and the UK seem to have found some kind of compromise at the 11th hour, at least for now,” Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec said, reporting from London.
“Strictly speaking, the consulate has shut its doors,” she said. “That’s in official language, but practically speaking, there is still a diplomatic presence that is going to be maintained in occupied East Jerusalem by the UK.”
That, she said, “allows both sides to essentially say that they’ve won the argument”.
“We absolutely are at a low point with UK-Israeli relations,” Nedelec said, adding that in a post on X, Saar listed measures including “shuttering that consulate, and he also cited banning some 12 MPs from entering Israel”.
“Gideon Saar also did say, though, that they are allies and that the intelligence sharing continues,” she added.
Israeli anger has been heightened by a resolution passed by the UK’s Green Party at its recent party conference, equating Zionism with “racism”. The party’s leader, Zack Polanski – who is also Jewish – was not present for the vote. However, he liked a post by Green Party member Gill Tavner after the vote, calling on opponents of the motion to “get over yourselves and move on”. “The decision is made. Sometimes they don’t go your way. If you’d prefer to be with genocidal Labour, maybe just go,” she wrote.
Nihad Abu Ghosh, a Palestinian journalist, told Al Jazeera from Ramallah that Israel’s reaction to rising opposition in the UK to its war on Gaza is “driven by the election context, and by its heightened stance towards those it sees as infringing on or undermining Israel’s sovereignty”.

articles.summary: Iran strikes tankers outside Hormuz in signs of expanding campaign  Euronews.comIran war live: Iranian media reports ‘massive explosions’ in Hormuz Strait  Al JazeeraTanker attacked off Qatar as Iran claims route transporting oil through strait of Hormuz will be ‘closed’  The GuardianAttacks on tankers in Hormuz hit highest of any week since start of Iran war, sources say  ReutersTanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says&nb...
articles.full_text:
Two commercial vessels were hit within 24 hours — one off Qatar, the first attack in that area in six months, and one off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman — as IRGC-affiliated outlets suggested Tehran had extended operations beyond the crucial strait.
Iran's armed forces struck two commercial tankers outside the Strait of Hormuz within 24 hours this week, in what appeared to be a deliberate expansion of attacks beyond the strait, as Iranian officials issued a fresh wave of warnings against the United States.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said several projectiles hit the oil and chemical tanker Acers, flagged in Antigua and Barbuda, 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal in Qatar on Wednesday. Casualties were reported.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel and said it was heading toward the Strait of Hormuz.
It was the first attack in that area in more than six months.
In a separate incident on Thursday, Vanguard reported a fire on a tanker some 40 kilometres off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman, which it identified as likely the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalgout.
The UKMTO had not recorded the incident, and the cause of the fire was not immediately clear. NASA's FIRMS fire-detection system confirmed the blaze, and US military aircraft — including two KC-46 tankers, a KC-135, a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and several helicopters — were over the area at the time.
Iran and media affiliated with the IRGC did not officially claim responsibility for either attack. IRGC-affiliated outlets implicitly suggested that Tehran had "extended the scope of its operations against commercial vessels that violate Iranian laws and regulations in the Strait of Hormuz to waters beyond the strait."
Both incidents fall outside the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and gas shipments normally pass. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began in late February, after Iran and the US imposed concurrent naval blockades.
"The distance between you and us is determined by our missiles," Acting Defence Minister Majid Ebn ol-Reza posted on X on Thursday.
"Yesterday the Gulf of Oman, today the Indian Ocean and tomorrow the Bay of Pigs. If you make a mistake, you will see a new set of dividing lines.," ol-Reza added in an apparent reference to a failed, US-backed military landing on the southwestern coast of Cuba from April 1961 aimed at overthrowing the communist government of Fidel Castro.
Yahya Rahim Safavi, a senior military adviser to Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, had earlier warned that if the US or Israel attacked Iran again, Tehran could extend the war "as far as the Indian Ocean or other places," adding that Iranian forces had prepared contingency plans for worst-case scenarios.
Ebn ol-Reza was appointed acting minister after Aziz Nasirzadeh, Iran's then defence minister, was killed on 28 February — the first day of the war — alongside several other military commanders. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has nominated Mehrdad Akhlaqi as a permanent replacement, and parliament is due to hold a confidence vote on 18 October.
Iran's army spokesman said separately that its forces were ready to carry out pre-emptive operations, if necessary, to prevent what he described as "any aggression or attack by the enemy."

RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (AFP) — The Houthis claimed a flurry of attacks on Saudi targets on Wednesday including firing a ballistic missile at Riyadh airport, as the group battles for territory in Yemen against government forces supported by the kingdom.
The Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen, captured swathes of coastal land from Yemen’s pro-government forces last month after the country’s civil war reignited in July.
The internationally recognized government this week declared a counter-offensive and claims to have uprooted Houthi fighters from strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.
But the Iran-backed Houthis say they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by Agence France-Presse (AFP) have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
“Our armed forces have just targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The strike was accurate, by God’s grace, and led to a disruption of air traffic,” Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said Wednesday in a post on X.
The Saudi-led military coalition that backs Yemen’s government said the missile was intercepted.
In a separate post the Houthis also said they targeted military supplies at a camp area near the airport in the Yemeni city of Aden, the interim capital for the government.
The Yemeni government’s Saba news agency reported missiles and drones targeting that airport.
Saree earlier said drones and missiles also targeted Saudi Arabia’s Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait and had “hit their targets accurately.”
It is the second time this week that the Houthis claimed to have attacked the main airport in the Saudi capital.
It is facing frequent temporary closures of its airspace, according to tracking website Flightradar24, but Saudi authorities have not publicly acknowledged the closures or confirmed any strikes targeting the facility.
‘Terrified’
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has been fighting the Houthis since 2015, and is now trying to roll back the group’s latest advance.
On Monday, the coalition said it was providing air support for the counter-offensive launched by the Yemeni government forces.
After a four-year ceasefire, Yemen’s civil war re-erupted in July. Last month the Houthis seized the entire western coastline along the Red Sea in the country’s deadliest fighting in years.
The renewed violence has also deepened the wider Middle East war, which has roiled world energy markets and snarled shipping routes in the region.
Yemen’s government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory — home to most of the country’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
On Tuesday sources on both sides told AFP that fighting across the country had killed more than 270 government troops and Houthi fighters over the past day alone.
The Yemen conflict has also caused a dire humanitarian crisis that left most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.
More than 184,000 people have been displaced by the latest fighting, according to the United Nations.
Mohammed, a 33-year-old charity worker who fled from Mocha to Aden, told AFP on Tuesday that “people there are terrified.”
“Life in Mocha has come to a complete standstill — there is no movement at all. The city has become a war zone,” he said.

Agencies
The World Trade Organization is sharply increasing its forecast for merchandise trade growth worldwide this year, more than doubling its earlier prediction to 3.9 percentas booming AI investments offset a hit from the war in the Middle East.
The Geneva-based trade body says global trade chugged along at a hearty pace, as supply chains adapted and AI-related spending poured in to provide "a powerful boost to goods trade.”
The revised forecast marks a big jump from an initial WTO forecast in this spring for 1.9 percent growth for merchandise trade. The figure excludes services trade. The trade body forecast growth next year of 4.1 percent, up from 2.9 percent predicted in March.
"The revision reflects evidence that global supply chains adapted to disruptions in energy and fertilizer markets, while strong investment in AI-related infrastructure boosted trade in AI-enabling goods,” WTO said.
Trade of oil and gas and fertilizer through the Persian Gulf was shaken after the US-Israeli war against Iran began inFebruary. WTO said merchandise trade grew 3.5 percent in the first half of the year, powered by the artificial intelligence market. "Demand for AI-enabling goods such as semiconductors and servers accounted for 47 percent of global merchandise trade growth in the first half of 2026, and trade in these products rose by 67 percent year-on-year, accelerating from the already rapid expansion seen in 2024 and 2025,” WTO said.
Robert Steiger, its chief economist, said WTO teams — like most forecastershave been "surprised” at the strength of the AI investment boom. They anticipated that strong growth in AI-enabling goods like electronics and computers would moderate over time because of already-high growth last year and "market saturation” eventually.
"This actually has not happened. Trade in AI-enabling goods grew 16 percent in value terms in 2024. It grew 31 percent in value terms in 2025, and it grew an astonishing 67 percent in the first half of 2026,” he told reporters at WTO headquarters.
Liquefied natural gas exports from the Middle East fell by 47 percent in the first half of the year, while crude oil exports dropped by nearly a quarter, WTO said. But shipments from other suppliers helped limit the decline to roughly 1 percent for LNG and about 6 percent for crude. WTO said it expects global GDP to grow 2.6 percent this year and 2.9 percent in 2027, even though it predicted that the Middle East conflict will continue to weigh on trade through higher energy prices and transport route disruptions.

articles.title: The Houthis, Bab el-Mandeb, and Maritime Transport - The Red Team Analysis Society
articles.summary: The Houthis, Bab el-Mandeb, and Maritime Transport  The Red Team Analysis Society
articles.full_text:
(Art direction and design; 
illustration created with 
AI: Jean-Dominique Lavoix-Carli)
Fighting rages in Yemen, as the strategic battle for control over Bab el-Mandeb, the West Coast, and its mountainous defense line intensifies. Whatever the immediate tactical outcome of these ongoing hostilities, a profound shift occurred in September 2026. On 10 September, the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha, strategically located on the Red Sea. Then, the next day, they captured the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands, Dhubab, and Perim (or Mayyun) Island, sitting directly in the middle of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. As a result, they gained physical territorial control over the strait, combining thus long-range threat projection with now direct presence astride the Strait, one of global trade’s primary chokepoints, the lock to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
This dramatic escalation contrasts sharply with the earlier phase. During the first months of the US-Israel-Iran war, the Ansar Allah (“Partisans of God”), also known as the Houthis – the principal armed group fighting Yemen’s internationally recognised government since 2014 – had remained rather remote from the conflict.
Houthi restraint ended on 13 July 2026, when their Sanaa airport was bombed to prevent an Iranian aircraft carrying Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) advisors from landing.1For this paragraph, among other sources, Yousef Mawry, “Leading Houthi threatens ‘siege’ on Saudi Arabia after Yemen airport attack“, Al Jazeera, 14 July 26. While Yemen’s internationally recognised government claimed responsibility for the attack, the Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, retaliating the same day with drone and missile strikes on Saudi Abha airport.
Since then, hostilities have escalated, raising fears of a broader Middle East conflagration.
Maritime traffic and thus supply chains are already greatly upset by the chaotic situation in the Strait of Hormuz. Transit through Bab-el Mandeb was already disrupted, but had been slowly moving towards normalisation. Against this backdrop, what are the potential impacts of the latest Houthi actions: are we about to witness another severe degradation of maritime navigation and seaborne trade, along with its inevitable cascading negative effects?
In the first part of this article we briefly present maritime trade and outline the key role of the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb within it. Then we turn to the Houthi maritime attacks since 7 October 2023, identifying five phases – the last one having started on 5 October 2026 – and look at the consequences for maritime transport. This allows us to outline a pattern. Finally, we look at the impacts of the changes in maritime transport ushered by the Houthi attacks. We focus on one such effect, the distance sailed, and its multiple consequences.
The key role of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in world trade
Since World War II, global merchandise trade has skyrocketed to reach USD 26.26 trillion in 2025, measured through exports, at current prices.2UNCTAD datahub – Merchandise: Trade – Annual – Last updated 19 Mar. 2026. In value, China represented 17.5% of global exports, the EU (extra-European trade) 13.8% of global merchandise exports and 12.9% of imports, and the U.S. 8.32% of exports and 15.9% of imports.3UNCTAD, Ibid.; WTO, Spotlight: Global trade developments and outlook – Annual Report 2026.
Maritime transport is vital for merchandise trade.4We often find the following estimates: Maritime transport represents over 80% of total global merchandise trade volume, e.g. UNCTAD, Launch of the Review of Maritime Transport 2025, and around 70% of total global merchandise trade in value. This seems to originate in the following statement: “With over 80 per cent of global trade by volume and more than 70 per cent of its value being carried on board ships and handled by seaports worldwide, the importance of maritime transport for trade and development cannot be overemphasized.”UNCTAD, Review of Maritime Transport 2017, p.x, 16. However, how these figures are reached is not detailed: trade flows are given in USD and maritime flows in tonnes, ton-miles and TEU. Indeed a maritime expert, Pablo Rodas-Martini asked the same question and pondered on the absence of real answer, “One question, many answers: How much of the world’s trade is carried by sea?“, 2019. 
As a result, the reality is that we know neither the share of maritime transport in global merchandise trade in volume nor in value. And, relatedly, we cannot trace its evolution nor performance. In 2024, maritime transport volumes reached 12720 million tons.5UNCTAD, Review of Maritime Transport 2025, 24 Sep 2025, using private firm database research Clarksons Research 2025. For 2026–2030, UNCTAD expects total seaborne trade to increase at an annual average of 2 per cent.6Ibid., p.8. The UN body singles out geopolitical risks, including in the Red Sea, as heightening uncertainty and risks for the future of trade in general and maritime transport in particular. Those should not, however, stop growth, but could dampen it.7Ibid., p. 7-8.
Maritime trade can be schematically summarized in the diagram below:
First, seaborne trade is usually measured in volume, most often metric tonnes and TEUs (Twenty-foot Equivalent Units), as well as ton-miles and TEU-miles, which also consider the distance the volume of cargo travels.8TEU = Twenty-foot Equivalent Unit: Standard unit for counting containers of various capacities and for describing the capacities of container ships or terminals. One 20 Foot ISO container (see heading 17 below) equals 1 TEU.” United Nations, Glossary for Transport Statistics 3rd Edition (EN), p. 68.
Ton-miles or TEU-miles: One ton of cargo or one TEU shipped over a distance of one mile. For example, If a ship carries 10,000 tons of cargo across 2,000 miles, it generates 20,000,000 ton-miles of shipping demand.
Then, seaborne trade is categorised according to segments of the maritime freight market and thus types of vessels.9The shares of each market below are calculated according to shipment data fro 2026 from IMF Portwatch, Economy Monitor, World – Data: UN Global Platform; PortWatch – last updated 25 Sept. 26.
Dry bulk shipping is the largest segment in volume. It is used for massive loose substances, for example, for ores, coal, grains, and fertilizers. In 2026, in volume, it represented on average 39.38% of all outgoing shipments.
Next come containers, used to transport goods packed in standardised containers, either 20-foot or 40-foot. In 2026, this market represented 30.10% of outgoing shipments.
Tankers follow. They are used for liquids or gas, such as oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), but also water. In 2026, they represented 27.49% of outgoing shipments.
Finally we have two smaller market segments: general cargo – for packaged goods and substances not fit for containers – and Roll-on/Roll-off (RORO) – where cargo is driven on and off a ship using ramps, instead of being lifted by cranes, which includes car-carrying ships. They represent, respectively, 2.56% and 0.47% of outgoing shipments.
In this article, we shall not dwell on tankers and energy transportation, which deserve specific analysis considering notably the chaotic situation around Hormuz.
Finally, trade for each type of market segment must consider the shipping route taken, i.e. the specific maritime path or network of lanes used by commercial vessels to transport cargo between ports. They are categorised according to the transiting volume. The three main routes are the East-West routes, subdivided as:
- Asia-Europe – Connecting Asia to Europe;
- Transpacific – Connecting Asia to North America, which includes three routes: Asia to US West Coast, Asia to US East Coast via the Panama Canal and Asia to US East Coast via the Suez Canal;
- Transatlantic – Connecting North America to Europe.
We then have the non-mainlane routes, as detailed on the diagram, and the inter-regional routes, which are increasingly important in terms of transiting volumes, considering notably inter-regional traffic within eastern Asia.
It is along these shipping routes that chokepoints come into play. Chokepoints are critical, narrow maritime passageways, often straits, that dictate ship sizes and whose operational status – whether open or closed – directly determines the commercial viability of global trade routes. Portwatch references 28 chokepoints throughout the world.10IMF Portwatch, Port Monitor: Chokepoints.
Whether a chokepoint is open or closed ripples upward and downward throughout the entire maritime sector then through trade to impact the entire economic and political system upon which our current world civilisation is built. Three years ago, as the dimensions of the Hamas attack on southern Israel were still becoming clear, I wrote in MoneyControl that the real surprise was not that an explosion had occurred, but where it had occurred.
For months before October 7, 2023, warning signs had been accumulating elsewhere: an extraordinary surge in settler violence in the occupied West Bank, repeated incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque, accelerating settlement construction and the arrival in government of some of the most uncompromising figures of Israel's religious right.
The assumption among many regional observers was that the next Palestinian explosion would come from the occupied West Bank, perhaps accompanied by unrest among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Instead, it burst through the fences surrounding Gaza and triggered a chain of events that continues to reorder the Middle East and international politics.
Few wars in the post-World War II period have transformed so many relationships and strategic calculations within three years.
What began on the Gaza-Israel frontier spread to Lebanon, Yemen and Syria before becoming part of a direct war involving Iran. It disrupted shipping through the Red Sea, pulled the United States back into a region Washington had hoped to deprioritize, stalled Saudi-Israeli normalization, disrupted India's ambitious plan for an economic corridor through Israel to Europe, and contributed to a search for new security arrangements in the Muslim world.
It has also brought about a profound change in Israel's international standing, particularly among younger Americans and Europeans, while putting Palestine back at the centre of a diplomatic agenda from which it had increasingly been excluded.
Some conclusions in my first assessment proved wrong or premature. Others look considerably more prescient three years later.
The central argument, however, has survived the test of these tumultuous years: it was never possible to construct a new Middle East by simply building around Palestine.
Ghost of 1973
There was a historical irony to October 7 that was apparent even on that first morning.
Amazingly, the attack took place at a time when Israeli strategists were discussing the 1973 Yom Kippur War on the occasion of its 50th anniversary. The Egyptian army in 1973 had surprised Israel by crossing the Suez Canal and breaking through Israeli positions in Sinai, destroying the country's illusion of invincibility that had taken hold after its overwhelming victory over Arab armies in the 1967 Six-Day War.
Fifty years later, Israeli intelligence suffered another catastrophic surprise.
How Hamas managed to penetrate one of the world's most heavily monitored borders, circumvent sophisticated cameras, sensors, drones and communications surveillance, and evade the attention of Unit 8200 and the Shin Bet became one of the defining questions of October 7.
The parallel with 1973 became even more striking with time.
The significance of the 1973 war lay not merely in what happened on the battlefield. The shock eventually changed political calculations. It helped create conditions in which Egypt and Israel could move towards the Camp David process and ultimately their 1979 peace treaty.
October 7 also shattered assumptions, but three years later it has yet to produce a comparable political settlement.
Instead, it has generated a much larger regional convulsion.
Israelis themselves are still demanding an independent inquiry into how October 7 was allowed to happen, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continues to face criticism over responsibility for the security and intelligence failures. On the third anniversary, protesters again gathered in Jerusalem demanding accountability ahead of Israel's October 27 election.
Second Front Turns Regional War
My October 2023 report also cited contacts between Hamas leaders in Beirut and Hezbollah and raised the possibility that an Israeli invasion of Gaza could produce a second front.
That prediction materialized, although on a scale considerably greater than envisaged at the time.
Fighting across the Lebanese border developed into a major confrontation with Hezbollah. The Houthis in Yemen began attacking Red Sea shipping and firing missiles and drones towards Israel, linking the Gaza conflict to one of the world's most important maritime trade routes. Israel repeatedly struck Syria and Yemen.
Eventually, the long-running shadow conflict between Israel and Iran, previously conducted through assassinations, cyber operations, sabotage and proxy forces, became an overt war.
The United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on February 28 this year, and the conflict has continued for more than six months, interrupted by periods of negotiation and renewed exchanges of fire. The Middle East that Washington hoped to stabilize sufficiently to reduce its military commitments instead became an interconnected battlefield stretching from the Mediterranean to the Persian Gulf.
October 7 did not by itself cause every subsequent conflict. The Israeli-Iranian confrontation, the war in Yemen and the rivalries in Syria all predated 2023. But Gaza acted as an accelerator that connected conflicts that had previously operated on separate tracks.
In an assessment published immediately after the Hamas attack, I made a deliberately provocative argument:
"Everyone has won, but at the cost of Palestinian lives."
Three years later, that sentence deserves to be revisited rather than defended.
I argued first that Iran had gained because the Abraham Accords and the anticipated Saudi-Israel normalization process had been derailed.
The United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Morocco retained diplomatic relations with Israel. But the larger strategic project that Washington hoped would culminate in Saudi recognition of Israel was halted.
Riyadh now insists that normalization cannot proceed without a credible pathway towards Palestinian statehood, something the present Israeli government rejects.
Iran therefore achieved one immediate strategic objective without firing the opening shot: the prospect of a Saudi-Israeli breakthrough disappeared from the diplomatic calendar.
I had also argued that Russia would benefit because international attention would move from Ukraine to the Middle East.
Gaza competed with Ukraine for diplomatic attention, Western political bandwidth and, importantly, military resources.
But Russia did not receive the uncomplicated strategic windfall that the first assessment suggested. Ukraine remained a central European security issue, while instability in the Middle East created new uncertainties for Moscow as well.
The more important point was that the United States suddenly had to divide attention among Europe, the Indo-Pacific and an increasingly combustible Middle East.
The third proposition concerned Washington.
Before October 7, the United States hoped to stabilize the Middle East sufficiently to shift greater strategic attention and military resources towards the Indo-Pacific and the long-term competition with China.
Washington was drawn into protecting Red Sea shipping, defending Israel, responding to attacks against American interests, and eventually participating directly in war against Iran.
China did gain the strategic breathing space I had anticipated, but the larger consequence was that America's hoped-for disengagement from Middle Eastern crises became impossible.
Even America's traditional security architecture in the Gulf is now being questioned. Gulf governments are examining alternative and supplementary arrangements as doubts grow over the durability of the U.S.-centred security umbrella.
Perhaps the most dramatic illustration of this altered strategic landscape is the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed on August 7 this year by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan.
Its central clause states that an armed attack against one of the three will be regarded as an attack against all. The three governments say the agreement is not directed against any country and builds on longstanding defence relationships, Islamic solidarity and common strategic interests.
Saudi-Pakistani defence cooperation is decades old, while Türkiye has long pursued greater strategic autonomy. The Iran war, the Yemen conflict and doubts about American security guarantees contributed directly.
Before October 7, one of Washington's principal regional objectives was to bring Saudi Arabia and Israel into a formal relationship. Three years later, Riyadh has instead entered a collective defence framework with Türkiye and nuclear-armed Pakistan.
Analysts examining the pact have explicitly connected the changing security landscape to October 7, Gaza, subsequent Israeli operations in the region, the fall of the Assad government and Red Sea instability.
The alliance is already moving beyond paper commitments. Türkiye is now providing Saudi Arabia with technical and defensive assistance as Riyadh confronts Houthi attacks, including air-defence support, intelligence sharing and logistics.
That represents a very different regional architecture from the one being imagined in Washington before October 7.
India's Grand Corridor Collapse
For India, the timing was particularly extraordinary.
Barely four weeks before the Hamas attack, Prime Minister Narendra Modi had joined American, European, Saudi, Emirati and other leaders at the G20 summit in New Delhi to announce the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, or IMEC.
New Delhi presented it with considerable fanfare as one of the great diplomatic achievements of its G20 presidency.
The concept was both economic and geopolitical. Indian goods would travel by sea to the Gulf, move by rail across the Arabian Peninsula towards Israel, and then travel from the Mediterranean to Europe.

U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday he would not authorize fresh military strikes against Iran ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, ruling out a resumption of attacks before Americans head to the polls
Trump, while stumping for Republicans this week, has hinted that was confident that at endgame to the war cold come in the days before or after the election, while also hinting that he remained open to resuming full-scale military operations against Iran.
But Trump in a social media post on Thursday said the U.S. "will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd."
Trump added that his team has been "having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran."
Negotiations had appeared at a standstill since Trump late last month publicly rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the U.S. met certain conditions.
Iran, however, said last week they had received a U.S. counterproposal. And Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Thursday said he expected Tehran would offer a formal reply within days.
Trump's post comes as the military has dispatched more resources to the region. U.S. officials have said a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, and thousands of troops aboard it and accompanying ships could arrive as early as the end of October.
Trump's announcement was made the same day the USS Abraham Lincoln was due to arrive to its home port in San Diego after a record-long deployment in support of the Iran war. There have been reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products.
The USS George Washington, which is usually based in Asia, relieved the Lincoln in August. The other aircraft carrier in the Middle East, the USS George H.W. Bush, has been deployed for about six months, but it pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for a port visit several days ago.

articles.summary: Massive 2,000-year-old discovery from time of Jesus emerges remarkably intact  Fox NewsAncient Jewish ritual bath from time of Jesus lifted intact from Israeli construction site  Washington TimesMassive 2,000-Year-Old Discovery Brings the World of Jesus to Life  Charisma Magazine Online2,000-Year-Old Jewish Ritual Bath Dating Back to Time of Jesus Unearthed in Israel  Yahoo
articles.full_text:
A remarkably intact 2,000-year-old Jewish ritual bath dating to around the time of Jesus has been unearthed in Israel — shedding light not only on Christ's life but also "illuminating the world of the Bible," according to a bestselling author and filmmaker.
The mikveh, which dates to the Second Temple period roughly 2,000 years ago, was recently extracted from Kiryat Gat, an Israeli city roughly 35 miles southwest of Jerusalem.
The structure had been uncovered during an archaeological excavation. The operation to remove it intact was announced by the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) in September.
Pictures released by officials show a massive crane lifting the 25-ton mikveh intact from the archaeological site.
Mikvehs, or Jewish ritual baths, are traditionally used for purification.
The bath dates roughly to the time of the life and ministry of Jesus Christ, who, as a Jew living during the Second Temple period, likely used mikvehs, though Scripture does not explicitly say that he did.
The mikveh is evidence that a Second Temple-period Jewish settlement, previously unknown to scholars, once existed in the area, according to officials.
Officials also noted that the excavation uncovered stone measuring vessels, which were widely used during the Second Temple period because, under Jewish law, they were not considered susceptible to ritual impurity.
The ancient structure is eventually expected to return to the community where it was found.
"The operation was carried out with the aim of protecting the ancient structure from damage during the neighborhood's development work," the IAA said in a statement.
"When construction is completed, the mikveh will be returned to the site, and integrated into an open public space that will stand at the heart of the new neighborhood."
The discovery helps bring the biblical world to life, according to Dinesh D'Souza, an author, commentator and Christian apologist who spoke to Fox News Digital about the find.
"It’s quite remarkable because I’ve seen these ritual baths, these mikveh[s]," D'Souza said.
"They’re usually pretty small."
He added, "It gives you a vivid picture. In some ways, it brings the Bible to life, both the Old Testament and the New, because this mikveh reflects the times right around the time of Jesus."
He added, "This is confirming, describing, illuminating the world of the Bible. That’s one of the things that biblical archaeology can do. It can authenticate the historicity of the Bible — not the theology, not the miracles, but the historicity of it."
D’Souza's new book, "The Stones Cry Out," as well as his documentary of the same name, were the result of extensive research into biblical archaeology. He pointed to the Pool of Siloam as a significant example of an ancient ritual bath with biblical connections.
"The Pool of Siloam connects to the temple by the Pilgrimage Road, a road on which almost certainly Jesus walked," D'Souza said.
"For me as a believer, it is chilling to sort of stand in these locations, observe them, walk the Pilgrimage Road, because in a sense you are connecting in a very experiential way with these profound artifacts of ancient times."
D'Souza said he sees a broader significance in biblical archaeology beyond what such discoveries reveal about ancient Israel.
"Western civilization and America are based on the sort of anchors or twin pillars of Athens and Jerusalem," he said. "To me, the archaeology of Jerusalem is supporting that Jerusalem pillar of Athens and Jerusalem."
"In other words, there is a relevance not just to Israel, but to Western civilization as a whole and specifically to America."

Israel announced Thursday that the British Consulate in East Jerusalem has "ceased to function," forcing 20 staffers to leave the country and deepening the worst diplomatic rift between the allies in decades.
The sign outside the consulate was taken down, but Britain said the building remains open and a core staff will continue to deliver "vital services” and work with Palestinians.
The U.K. government said it would not retaliate by expelling Israeli diplomats as it seeks to rebuild its staff.
The dispute began last month when the United Kingdom banned trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The United Nations and much of the international community consider all settlements as illegal.
"Israel will no longer turn its cheek to diplomatic attacks against it," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said in a statement, adding that the building would continue to operate with a "task force" of seven diplomats and a "very limited” scope of activity. Twenty British diplomats will leave Israel, including the consul general.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement that the building "will be known as the U.K. Mission, Jerusalem" after discussions with Israel’s government, and a small team of diplomats would continue to operate there.
"This will ensure that we maintain our longstanding British presence and the U.K.'s role in support of a two-state solution," Miliband added.
Britain had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats if the consulate was closed, but said it would not do so for now because it's in talks with Israel about expanding the mission.
"We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence," Miliband said.
Meanwhile, "our diplomats are going to be able to carry out their important work in relation to, for example, relations with the Palestinians, but also supporting British nationals visiting the area," Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty told Times Radio.
Miliband made clear that Britain does "not accept that the government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, which has been there for nearly 200 years."
The foreign secretary added that the U.K. government reiterates its view that East Jerusalem "is occupied territory."
The U.K. and Israel continue to have close defense and security cooperation, but diplomatic relations have deteriorated over Israel’s conduct of its genocidal war on Gaza and Britain’s decision last year to recognize a Palestinian state.
Last month’s announcement of the ban on trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank marked a significant toughening of Britain’s stance toward a longtime ally.
Doughty, the Middle East minister, said the U.K. has "a strong and ongoing relationship with Israel."
Israel captured and occupied the West Bank, along with Gaza and East Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war, territories the Palestinians want for a future state.
Since then, the Israeli government has built scores of settlements that are home to well over 500,000 illegal Jewish settlers. Many settlements resemble fully developed suburbs.

Memorial events have taken place in Israel on the third anniversary of the devastating Hamas-led attack there that sparked the war in Gaza.
Families paid tribute to their loved ones at some of the sites where about 1,200 people were killed in the assault and 251 were taken hostage.
"The nation unites on this day in the longing for our dear ones," said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faced calls from protesters for an independent state inquiry into security failures that day.
In response to the attack, Israel launched a military offensive in Gaza which has killed more than 74,200 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN.
Violence has continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed almost a year ago and living conditions for the 2.1 million people living there remain dire.
On Wednesday morning, bereaved families and survivors gathered at a memorial for the 378 people who were killed at the Nova dance festival in southern Israel on 7 October 2023.
The festival site was near Kibbutz Re'im and not far from the border with Gaza, from where Hamas-led gunmen launched their dawn attack.
Witnesses have described how festival-goers were shot, sexually abused and tortured by gunmen during the raid.
Forty-four people were kidnapped, of whom 25 were brought back from Gaza alive.
Ahuva Yavin Mayze, whose 21-year-old daughter Adi was shot and killed at Nova, told the BBC what happened at the site was "dystopic, unimaginable".
"Today is a difficult day, not only for me but for a large part of the nation," said Shlomo Sharf, a former Israeli footballer, in comments reported by Channel 12.
He paid tribute to his granddaughter, May Naim, 24, who was also killed at the festival.
Former hostage Yarden Bibas, whose wife and two young sons were kidnapped from their home in Kibbutz Nir Oz and later killed in captivity in Gaza, was quoted by the Times of Israel as saying: "Shiri, Ariel and Kfir. Sorry. Sorry that you are up there and I am here."
Crowds also filed into the small cemetery at Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where 64 residents were killed and 19 were taken hostage on 7 October.
Zion Regev, a community leader, said most surviving residents had yet to return to their homes because of the trauma of what happened.
"This is the first time we are doing all the things here in the kibbutz," he told Reuters news agency. "It's a very emotional day, it's a very difficult day for our community, three years after 7 October."
A man who reportedly helped to fend off Hamas attackers at Kibbutz Magen praised IDF troops who "fought so bravely" during the raid.
Speaking to crowds at the national memorial event at Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park on Wednesday evening, Ido Yakir said Israel would remember everyone "who knew that they had to give their lives in order to save others".
In a statement released by his office on Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu said he had lit a memorial candle commemorating every victim of 7 October.
"We will complete the mission: we have settled the score and will continue settling the score with all the murderers," he added.
At a ceremony on Monday marking the Jewish calendar's anniversary of the attack, the prime minister said Israel had killed 4,000 out of the 6,000 Palestinians who infiltrated Israel from Gaza that day.
In Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Square, Israeli anti-government protesters dyed the fountain red to mark the anniversary of the attack.
The fountain has been used as a memorial site for those killed, with pictures, flowers and messages laid around the basin wall.
Protesters also briefly blocked one of the main highways in the city to hold a moment of silence on Wednesday morning.
They held banners that read, "the people will remember their sons and daughters", along with others that said "a complete failure" and "guilty" next to an image of Netanyahu.
Many senior Israeli defence and security officials have resigned or been fired since the attack took place. But there has not been an independent commission of inquiry into Israel's worst security failure.
The prime minister has rejected any personal responsibility and has refused to establish a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.
Einav Zangauker became an outspoken critic of the Netanyahu government while her son, Matan, was in captivity in Gaza. He was released last October as part of the ceasefire agreement.
"They're trying to make us forget what happened on 7 October," she told Army Radio. "We won't forget, we will demand the truth."
Memorial events were organised in other countries around the world, including in Germany, where the Jewish students' union held a vigil at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Hamas-led attack marked a "profound rupture".
"We commemorate the victims, we share their pain," he said, adding that antisemitism must be confronted with "even greater resolve".
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Britain's Jewish community: "We stand with you."
"The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day," he said.
Outside Downing Street, a vigil was also held to commemorate British-Israelis killed in the initial attack, later as hostages, or in fighting with Hamas.
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said: "The unspeakable savagery and terror of 7 October must never happen again."
She also said that the European Union "remains ready to help turn today's fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution."
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Wednesday, US President Donald Trump said he had spoken to Netanyahu and wished the people of Israel well.
"That was a horrible day, a horrible tragedy," he said.
This is the first anniversary of the 7 October attack with no hostages remaining in Gaza, but a US-brokered ceasefire deal from last year has failed to deliver peace or bring security.
There has been no end to Gaza's deadliest ever war, as Israel continues to carry out near-daily attacks.
More than 1,460 people have been killed there since the ceasefire took effect, according to Gaza health ministry. The Israeli military says at least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in the strip over the same period.
Most of Gaza is in ruins, with nearly all the 2.1 million population still displaced amid dire humanitarian conditions.
An estimated 80% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, leaving more than 60 million tonnes of rubble piled up and 1.2 million people living in tents or shelters, according to the UN.
Families who have been displaced several times during the war increasingly ask where they could go next, and whether they might even be forced to leave Gaza altogether.
Mohammed Emad al-Din, a 38-year-old father of two who works as a barber in Gaza City, said he had been displaced five times. His home was destroyed and his barber shop was partially damaged.
He told the BBC that the fear of being forced out of Gaza now follows him even into his dreams.
"I don't believe Israel caused all this destruction for nothing," he said.
"They have turned Gaza into a place that is almost impossible to live in, and I fear that we will eventually end up outside the place where we were born."
Another displaced Palestinian, Atta Saeed Hassan Shweikh, told the BBC that his son, daughter, sister and her children had all been killed during the war.
Speaking from Gaza City, he said Palestinians were "living in graves while still alive" and have endured "severe suffering".
At least three Palestinians were killed in Israeli strikes in the northern town of Beit Lahia and the southern city of Khan Younis on Wednesday, medics said.
The Israeli military said it struck two Hamas operatives in northern Gaza overnight, one of whom it accused of planting explosives near the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the territory still occupied by Israeli forces.
Hamas - which is proscribed as a terrorist organisation by Israel, the UK and others - released a statement praising the 7 October attack as a "historic milestone" in its "ongoing struggle project".
The statement, attributed to the group and disseminated in Palestinian media, called the attack "a natural response" to "bitter suffering" imposed by Israel.
