articles.title: Iranian protester hanged hours after marrying his imprisoned fiancée over jail phone line - Fox News
articles.summary: Iranian protester hanged hours after marrying his imprisoned fiancée over jail phone line  Fox NewsSpared, married, hanged: the last weeks of Iranian protester Alireza Sepahi  YahooTill death us do part: Iran’s prisoners marry before the gallows  The TimesIran protester recounts torture, mock execution after January arrest  Iran InternationalIranian January Protester Sentenced to Death in Shirvan Following Torture  IranWire
articles.full_text:
An Iranian anti-regime protester was hanged at dawn Oct. 5 inside Isfahan Central Prison, just hours after marrying his imprisoned fiancée over a jail phone line, The Times reported Thursday.
Alireza Sepahi, 25, was executed alongside co-defendant Alireza Raisi after being sentenced to death in the anti-government demonstrations at Isfahan’s Alikhani Square Jan. 8., according to Human Rights Iran.
Sepahi and his bride, student activist Mahshad Keshani, 22, knew and loved each other before being arrested during anti-regime demonstrations, the report said.
Keshani, who is serving a five-year sentence, pushed for an informal wedding Sunday as fears mounted that Sepahi’s execution was imminent after a final family summons.
The couple exchanged vows over the phone from inside Isfahan prison, joined by their fathers.
Human rights lawyer Amirsalar Davoudi facilitated the ceremony by reading the vows for the fathers to bless.
Keshani’s family gave a copy of the Quran, a saffron rock candy and a single red rose as a traditional dowry.
"It was Mahshad’s idea," Davoudi told The Times. "Even now, I wonder how one young woman can possess such courage."
Davoudi recalled warning Keshani about the permanent nature of the decision.
"I told her, ‘My dear, you understand that this cannot simply be undone?’" Davoudi said.
"She said, ‘Mr Davoudi, I love Alireza.’"
When Davoudi presented the proposal to Sepahi, the young man broke down in tears.
"Alireza was crying, and something deeply painful and beautiful happened. Even the prison officers began to cry," Davoudi said.
The ceremony held no formal authority to halt the execution. Sepahi had previously survived a scheduled hanging in July after suffering a heart attack on his way to the gallows. Authorities then rescheduled the execution after he regained consciousness.
On Monday morning, hours after the vows were spoken, Sepahi was hanged.
He is among seven defendants executed in the Alikhani Square case, in which 12 men were accused in the deaths of four security personnel.
After the hanging, Sepahi’s family was reportedly prevented by authorities from burying their son in his hometown.
Davoudi condemned the Iranian regime's actions.
"I do not know how to come to terms with this," Davoudi said.
"The regime is taking revenge on innocent young people for the humiliation it has suffered internationally."
Human rights groups report Keshani remains in custody, facing additional security charges.
This came as Maryam Rajavi, president-elect of the National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI), urged U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres to take immediate international action to halt executions and the killing of protesters in Iran, citing thousands of executions and decades of impunity for human rights abuses.
In a letter ahead of World Day Against the Death Penalty on Oct. 10, Rajavi called for international accountability, independent investigations and diplomatic and economic pressure on Tehran to end the executions.

articles.title: Rubio Says Iran Missed Nuclear Deal Opportunities - SuaraGarut.ID
articles.summary: Rubio Says Iran Missed Nuclear Deal Opportunities  SuaraGarut.ID
articles.full_text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran has missed multiple opportunities for a nuclear agreement as Washington and Tehran remain at an impasse, while fighting involving Iran-backed forces in Yemen and disputes over Gaza add pressure across the Middle East.
Rubio said Iran had rejected several chances to reach an agreement over its nuclear program during a visit to Greece, according to CNBC. The nuclear issue remains central to U.S. demands for a lasting ceasefire.
"Iran has failed to take advantage of multiple opportunities to reach agreement with us on nuclear program," said Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of State.
CNBC reported that Tehran disputes Washington's position. A senior Iranian official involved in indirect talks said there had been no negotiations on the nuclear program and that U.S. proposals conflicted with Iran's position.
"Iran will never give up its right to enrich, but enrichment details can be discussed later," said the senior Iranian official, according to Reuters as reported by CNBC.
Vice President J.D. Vance has said any agreement ending the seven-month conflict must include a meaningful reduction in Iran's nuclear enrichment. President Donald Trump previously denied reports that he offered sanctions relief in exchange for nuclear concessions.
In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthis have faced a counteroffensive along the southwestern coast while increasing pressure around Taiz, according to Iran International. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan also activated the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement after an emergency meeting in Riyadh.
"I think it’s too early to talk about sustainable gains against the Houthis at this point," said Thomas Juneau, a Yemen expert and non-resident fellow at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies.
"I think we need more time to see the dust settle," Juneau said.
Iran International reported that Houthi forces retain control of Hodeidah on the Red Sea coast, while Saudi-led coalition forces have struck military infrastructure in the governorate. The Houthis' proximity to maritime routes remains a concern even if their territorial position changes.
"If it turns out that the losses are limited to the southwest corner of Yemen, that is not surprising in the sense that that was difficult for the Houthis to hold," said Juneau.
"So that would not be a strategic setback for them," Juneau said.
Fatima Abo Alasrar said the Houthis' September advance had received support from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and benefited from poor coordination among Saudi-backed Yemeni forces.
"The biggest takeaway is that this myth of Houthi invincibility is no longer there," said Fatima Abo Alasrar, a Yemeni scholar, senior policy analyst and founder of Ideology Machine.
"Bab al-Mandab was just the icing on the cake," Abo Alasrar said.
She said attacks alone can raise shipping and insurance costs, making Hodeidah a more consequential strategic position. Taiz presents a different battlefield because of its dense population and the potential for prolonged fighting.
"What I’m watching right now is the population centers," said Abo Alasrar. "It’s in the cities, it’s in the population centers that the Houthis can inflict real damage."
Juneau cautioned against concluding that the Houthis are suffering sustained losses based only on the coastal fighting.
"I don’t think we’re in a position to say yet that the Houthis are sustaining losses," said Juneau.
Mohammed al-Basha said the Yemen conflict is connected to the wider confrontation with Iran but retains separate local dynamics involving its own actors, grievances and battlefields.
"The war in Yemen is unlikely to end without a broader resolution to the war with Iran," said Mohammed al-Basha, a Yemeni-American analyst and founder of the Basha Report.
"But ending the confrontation in the Strait of Hormuz will not, by itself, end the war in Yemen," al-Basha said.
"The two conflicts are interconnected, but they are also distinct, with their own actors, grievances, battlefields, and political dynamics," al-Basha said.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan said implementing their defense agreement would strengthen collective deterrence and accelerate deployment of agreed military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.
"This is an important signal. It is a deterrent signal," said Abo Alasrar.
In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani also addressed tensions surrounding the Gaza war after attending a vigil marking the October 7, 2023, attacks. His statement said Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others.
"We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss," Mamdani said.
He then described the subsequent war in Gaza and cited more than 74,000 Palestinian deaths, including more than 21,000 children, while defending his decision to attend the vigil despite protests.
"I was proud to attend last night's vigil, as I did last year, to listen to testimonies from family members of those who were killed on Oct. 7 and those who've been killed in the three years since, and all of whom united in a vision for peace and an end to the genocide in Gaza. And when we're speaking of that genocide, we're speaking of one that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in the last three years," Mamdani said.
"As for those protesting me, I am the mayor of New York City, and this is what I signed up for," Mamdani said.
"And I've been very clear, both as a candidate as well as the mayor of our city, of my firm belief that we have to extend human rights to all people and that has to include Palestinians. And that as Americans, we have a special responsibility, given our federal government's complicity in funding so much of the weaponry that has been used over these last three years," Mamdani said.
"And we also know that when we are commemorating the anniversary, three years of horrific war crimes, three years since Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted hundreds more, three years of an anniversary that has brought unthinkable devastation to so many that also the Israeli government used and continues to use that day, those war crimes, as a justification for an ongoing genocide against Palestinians," Mamdani said.
"This is something that has shattered the lives of so many New Yorkers, whether in those who I was standing alongside at the vigil, recounting their own family members who were killed, or reading the testimonies of Palestinians whose family members have been killed, or the then-Palestinian New Yorkers that I met soon after that vigil who shared with me — for example, a Palestinian-Christian nurse here in New York City sharing with me that she lost 17 of her family members when the Israeli military bombed a church," Mamdani said.

articles.summary: UAE Cyber Security Council, SCC Plan Cyber Resilience Centre  PCMag Middle East
articles.full_text:
The UAE Cyber Security Council and SCC Middle East plan to develop a Centre of Excellence for Cyber Resilience and Trusted Technology in the UAE. The partners announced the proposal on Oct. 6 at AI Everything Abu Dhabi, but didn’t give a launch date or name a specific location.
The centre is intended to bring government agencies, businesses, technology partners, and specialists together to test use cases and assess how emerging technologies can be adopted securely, according to the announcement. The partners describe it as a place to work on practical deployments, rather than simply showcase products.
The planned work has three phases:
- Build national capability: Executive learning, practical labs, and specialist development in AI, cloud, data, cybersecurity, and critical national infrastructure.
- Incubate UAE innovation: A startup program to develop and test locally created cybersecurity technologies against real-world requirements.
- Connect with international markets: Support for selected UAE-developed technologies seeking overseas customers, partners, and commercial opportunities.
The Council and SCC Middle East said they’ll lead integration and delivery, drawing on expertise and resources according to each program’s needs. The announcement doesn’t specify how startups will be selected, what training will cost, or which technology partners will take part.
“The harder question is how you bring the right technologies together, prove they work for the environment you are putting them into and then turn that into a real outcome,” SCC Middle East CEO Daniel Valle said. He described the centre as a place to test ideas and build solutions that can be deployed. UAE Government Head of Cyber Security Dr. Mohamed Al Kuwaiti said it would help government, industry, and technology partners turn the country’s digital ambitions into practical capability.
There’s no information yet on funding, enrollment, public access, or the first technologies to be tested. The release also doesn’t say whether the centre will operate from a single facility or across existing partner sites. For companies in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt, those details will determine whether the initiative offers hands-on programs, commercial partnerships, or both.
Part of a wider UAE technology push
The proposal fits with other regional efforts to build technology capacity. In September 2026, TahawulTech reported that the Council and Fortinet had launched an internship program for Emirati cybersecurity talent, with training, practical labs, and mentorship. That program focuses on developing people; the new centre’s stated scope also includes startup incubation and international market access.
The UAE has also seen announcements around AI infrastructure, including an AI centre planned by e& and Intel in Dubai. Separately, OpenAI’s cybersecurity work has drawn attention to AI tools aimed at security teams, as covered in a report on its restricted security AI. Those efforts have different purposes, but show why the new centre’s testing and training plans matter: organizations need ways to assess technologies in the environments where they’ll be used.
The UAE Cyber Security Council has also worked on public cybersecurity awareness. In September 2025, Aljundi reported that the Council and Abu Dhabi Police warned residents about unknown calls and messages used in phishing and fraud. The proposed centre targets a different audience, but its focus on secure adoption puts practical testing alongside that public-facing work.

articles.title: Could Kuwait be the next country to join the Abraham Accords? - opinion - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Could Kuwait be the next country to join the Abraham Accords? - opinion  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
If Kuwait is moving toward normalization with Israel, the consequences could extend far beyond another diplomatic agreement, reshaping calculations from Riyadh to Tehran.
Sometimes, in the Middle East, what is not announced matters more than what is.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s unusually quiet visit to Abu Dhabi to meet UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed raises an obvious question: Why now, and why so quietly?
There was no public agenda, no joint press conference, and no diplomatic fanfare. Netanyahu flew to the UAE, met MBZ, and returned to Israel several hours later, with little explanation of what had been discussed.
That silence may be the most interesting part of the story.
My suspicion is that the meeting was about more than another bilateral consultation. Kuwait may be part of a larger conversation behind closed doors, possibly involving the next expansion of the Abraham Accords.
Less than two weeks earlier, Israel’s ambassador to the UAE, Yossi Shelley, suggested publicly that another country could join the accords within four to six months. He specifically pointed to Kuwait.
Kuwait has traditionally been among the Gulf states most cautious toward normalization with Israel and has long maintained a public position opposed to it. That is precisely why a Kuwaiti move would matter so much.
Neutrality does not stop a missile
Iran has made the threat facing the Gulf impossible to treat as theoretical.
The events of 2026 showed how quickly a confrontation involving Tehran can spill across borders. Iranian missiles and drones reached Gulf states, including Kuwait, forcing governments that had tried to balance relations with Washington and Tehran to confront an uncomfortable reality.
Neutrality does not stop a missile. Diplomatic caution does not intercept a drone. Geography does not disappear because a government would prefer to remain outside somebody else’s war.
Kuwait sits close to Iran, hosts a major American military presence, and occupies a strategically sensitive position at the northern edge of the Gulf.
That changes Israel’s strategic value in Gulf calculations.
Israel possesses capabilities Gulf governments increasingly need: combat-tested missile defense, sophisticated intelligence, early-warning systems, cyber capabilities, and years of experience confronting Iranian weapons and proxies.
The question is no longer simply whether Gulf capitals approve of Israeli policy. It is whether they can build the next regional security architecture without Israel.
The Abraham Accords began as diplomatic normalization. Their next phase may be about shared early warning, intelligence coordination, missile and drone defense, maritime security, and protection of critical infrastructure.
This is where MBZ becomes central. The UAE maintains deep relations with Washington, has built an extensive partnership with Israel, and keeps channels open to regional rivals. Abu Dhabi also has an interest in a Gulf where security relationships are increasingly interconnected. Bringing Kuwait closer to the Abraham Accords would fit that strategy.
The road from Kuwait City leads to Riyadh
A Kuwaiti move would also change the strategic context surrounding Saudi Arabia, the most consequential potential addition to the Abraham Accords.
This would not mean Riyadh would automatically follow. Saudi Arabia has its own interests and its own position on the Palestinian issue.
But Kuwait would remove another political and psychological barrier. If even Kuwait can establish relations with Israel, the definition of what is politically possible in the Gulf changes.
Saudi policymakers would increasingly have to consider not only what normalization would require, but also the implications of remaining outside a regional network that is gradually becoming more integrated.
Such a network would not be an Arab-Israeli NATO. What could emerge is something looser: states that do not agree on everything but increasingly share intelligence, technology, warning systems, and maritime interests.
The United States would remain indispensable. Washington provides military reach and security guarantees no regional power can replace. The Abraham Accords provide a framework through which regional cooperation can deepen.
Iran’s strategic paradox
For Tehran, this is the greater danger.
An Israeli flag flying over another embassy in the Gulf is symbolic. Israeli radar, intelligence, early-warning systems, and security coordination becoming embedded in the Gulf are something else entirely.
For decades, Iran benefited from a regional structure in which Israel and Gulf Arab states shared concerns about Tehran while remaining politically separated. The Abraham Accords began to close that strategic space. Iran’s own behavior may now be closing it further.
Every missile launched toward a Gulf state strengthens the argument for integrated air defense. Every drone attack strengthens the case for shared early warning. Every threat to shipping strengthens the argument for maritime coordination.
And every demonstration of Iranian reach makes Israeli intelligence and defense technology more relevant to governments that once saw relations with Israel primarily as a political liability.
That is Tehran’s strategic paradox: In demonstrating its ability to threaten the region, Iran may be accelerating the construction of the very regional architecture it has spent years trying to prevent.
Watch the silence
Perhaps Kuwait was not discussed in Abu Dhabi. Perhaps Netanyahu and MBZ were simply conducting another strategic consultation.
But the timing is difficult to ignore.
An Israeli ambassador publicly identifies Kuwait as a possible new member of the Abraham Accords. Less than two weeks later, Netanyahu quietly travels to Abu Dhabi for an unexplained meeting with a leader who helped turn Arab-Israeli normalization into a regional strategy.
That may be a coincidence.
I suspect it is not. In chess, you do not always announce what comes next. Sometimes you quietly reposition the pieces, create pressure, and wait for your opponent to understand what has changed. The decisive move is often prepared several turns before its purpose becomes clear.
The original Abraham Accords showed that Arab states did not have to wait for a final Israeli-Palestinian settlement before establishing relations with Israel. A Kuwaiti move would suggest something more: that the strategic logic behind normalization has become powerful enough to reach one of the Gulf states most resistant to it.
The first phase of the Abraham Accords was about recognition. The next may be about integration.
Perhaps that is what was being discussed behind closed doors in Abu Dhabi.
And perhaps the quietest meeting in the Gulf this week will eventually prove to have been one of its loudest moves.
Liron Rose is an entrepreneur, co-founder of the Masad Haaretz Institute, and creator and host of the geopolitical podcasts Israel Insider and HaYanshuf.
Amit Shabi is a former analyst in Intelligence Unit 8200, an investment and capital markets professional, author of several finance books, and a competitive chess player.

articles.title: ExxonMobil’s growing global LNG portfolio strengthens its ability to serve energy markets around the world - Energy Connects
articles.summary: ExxonMobil’s growing global LNG portfolio strengthens its ability to serve energy markets around the world  Energy Connects
articles.full_text:
Global energy markets are evolving, and liquefied natural gas (LNG) continues to play an increasingly important role in meeting rising energy demand, supporting economic development, and enhancing energy security around the world.
With more than 50 years of LNG experience, ExxonMobil is building on its strong foundation to expand its global LNG portfolio and strengthen its ability to connect reliable supply with growing demand across key markets.
From helping pioneer LNG developments in the 1970s to supporting the growth of LNG markets in Korea and India, participating in major ventures in Qatar and Papua New Guinea, and developing import infrastructure across Europe, Asia, and the Americas, ExxonMobil has played an important role in the evolution of the global LNG industry.
Today, the company is focused on the next chapter of that journey. Through strategic investments in LNG projects and infrastructure, ExxonMobil is expanding its portfolio to help meet customer needs and support growing demand for reliable energy.
The company’s LNG portfolio is on track to nearly double by 2030 through developments in the United States, Qatar, Papua New Guinea, and Mozambique, creating one of the industry’s most diverse and geographically advantaged LNG portfolios.
A key part of this growth is Golden Pass LNG, ExxonMobil’s joint venture with QatarEnergy on the US Gulf Coast. The project will connect abundant US natural gas resources with customers around the world through three liquefaction trains, adding significant new LNG supply to global markets and strengthening ExxonMobil’s ability to serve customers for decades to come.
ExxonMobil Head of Global LNG Trading, Sid Bambawale, says the delivery of ExxonMobil’s first LNG cargo from the project to Asia aboard the HL Sea Eagle in June 2026 marked an important milestone for the company’s expanding LNG business.
“The delivery of our first cargo from Golden Pass represents an important step in the continued growth of ExxonMobil’s LNG portfolio,” Bambawale says.
“By combining world-class LNG assets, shipping capabilities, and deep experience across global energy markets, we are strengthening our ability to reliably deliver LNG to customers around the world and help meet growing energy demand.”
Beyond Golden Pass, ExxonMobil continues to advance LNG opportunities in Papua New Guinea, Mozambique, and Australia. Together with regasification capacity in the United Kingdom, Europe, and China, these investments create a broad and geographically diverse portfolio capable of serving customers across multiple regions.
This expanding network provides ExxonMobil with the flexibility to respond to changing customer requirements and evolving market conditions while maintaining a focus on reliable supply.
As LNG demand continues to grow across Asia, Europe, and emerging markets, the company’s portfolio is increasingly well-positioned to connect LNG resources with the markets that need them most.
Commenting at Gastech in Bangkok, Bambawale highlighted the importance of engaging directly with customers and industry participants.
“Events like Gastech provide an important opportunity to connect with customers, partners, and stakeholders across the LNG value chain,” Bambawale says.

articles.title: What happened to NEOM’s “flying” stadium, suspended 350 metres above the ground? - Domus Web
articles.summary: What happened to NEOM’s “flying” stadium, suspended 350 metres above the ground?  Domus Web
articles.full_text:
First came Riyadh’s gigantic cube, The Mukaab, then The Line, the 170-kilometre-long city planned in the heart of the desert. Now, NEOM Stadium—the “flying” stadium that was supposed to be one of 15 venues for the 2034 FIFA World Cup—could also be on hold. One after another, some of the megaprojects envisioned by Saudi Arabia as part of Vision 2030—the national programme unveiled in 2016 under the leadership of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to diversify the country’s economy and reduce its dependence on oil—are being scaled back, delayed or put on hold altogether.
What happened to NEOM’s “flying” stadium, suspended 350 metres above the ground?
After The Line and The Mukaab, Saudi Arabia may have also put its plans for NEOM Stadium on hold. The suspended venue was supposed to host the 2034 FIFA World Cup, and its uncertain future is perhaps the clearest sign yet of how NEOM itself is changing.
View Article details
- Alessia Baranello
- 08 October 2026
Designed to sit 350 metres above the ground, with a capacity of 46,000 spectators and an estimated cost of $2.5 billion, NEOM Stadium made headlines online when its first renderings were released. The project has now reportedly been put on hold indefinitely. Reuters reported the news, citing two people familiar with the matter. MEED Projects, a platform specialising in tracking major construction projects across the Middle East, also lists the stadium as “on hold” and no longer gives an expected completion date.
The Line slows down, and so does its stadium
The fate of NEOM Stadium was closely tied to that of The Line and NEOM, the Saudi megaproject for urban, industrial and infrastructure development along the Red Sea, of which the linear city was intended to be a central component. The stadium had been conceived as an integral part of The Line itself: it would be embedded into the city 350 metres above ground and powered entirely by renewable energy.
The slowdown of The Line is therefore affecting its stadium as well. In April, Reuters reported that Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, had said The Line was no longer a priority and that there was no need to complete its first phase by 2030. The Red Sea utopia had already been significantly scaled back from its original vision. The stadium’s fate, however, does not amount to an official cancellation. NEOM and the Saudi government’s media office did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment, while Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Sport referred questions to the World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority.
The authority said major progress was already being made on infrastructure for the tournament, but did not directly address questions about NEOM Stadium or its costs.
From utopian city to industrial platform
The fate of the stadium is part of a much broader shift affecting NEOM as a whole: investment is moving away from its cultural and urban infrastructure and increasingly towards industrial, energy and digital projects, including Oxagon, the new port hub on the Red Sea, and the data centres appearing in the project’s latest masterplans. In this sense, the slowdown of NEOM Stadium is simply the most spectacular symbol of a transformation that was already underway.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia since 7 October: From the push for normalisation to strategic hedging - نون بوست
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia since 7 October: From the push for normalisation to strategic hedging  نون بوست
articles.full_text:
In September 2023, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke confidently of the kingdom moving “every day” closer to a historic US-brokered agreement with “Israel.” The terms seemed almost settled: a defence treaty with Washington, a civilian nuclear programme and little more than promises to the Palestinians, in exchange for Saudi recognition. The deal would mark the culmination of the process begun by the “Abraham Accords” and give them the Islamic standing they lacked.
A few weeks later, the events of 7 October swept those plans aside. The war on Gaza, followed by the US-Israeli war on Iran that began in February 2026, forced Riyadh to reassess its regional strategy. For years, the kingdom had relied exclusively on US protection and treated normalisation as a means of securing it. It emerged from the two wars with a different doctrine: hedging its bets, balancing relations with competing powers and building regional alliances to protect its strategic interests from shifts in Washington’s policy and Tel Aviv’s military adventurism.
The rising public and political cost of normalisation
Saudi Arabia’s pragmatic case for rapid normalisation rested on an implicit assumption: the Palestinian cause could no longer mobilise public opinion, and younger Saudis, preoccupied with Vision 2030 projects, no longer cared about events in Gaza and the West Bank.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza shattered that assumption. Images of widespread destruction and starvation, alongside casualty figures exceeding those of the region’s previous conflicts, revived concern for Palestine across Arab societies, including Saudi Arabia, and even in the West, with an intensity that entire generations had never witnessed. The term “genocide” became prominent in international forums, courtrooms and US and European media. Arab leaders could no longer shake hands with those implicated without seriously damaging their domestic standing.
For Saudi Arabia, the cost extends beyond public opinion. The kingdom derives a substantial part of its legitimacy from its custodianship of the Two Holy Mosques and its standing in the Islamic world. Drawing closer to an Israeli government deeply implicated in genocide and crimes against humanity, whose ministers openly advocate displacement and changes to the status quo at Al-Aqsa Mosque, would undermine that religious and political standing. It would also hand an advantage to Riyadh’s regional rivals, who are waiting for any opportunity to damage its image.
This explains the most significant change in official Saudi rhetoric. Promises to improve Palestinian lives or offer a vague route to statehood were no longer sufficient. A credible, irreversible path to an independent Palestinian state on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital, became a precondition for recognition.
Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan reiterated that position in New York a few days ago, stressing the need to translate international consensus on the two-state solution into practical steps to ensure its implementation. The condition helps Riyadh resist repeated US pressure and incentives. It sets a requirement the current Israeli government cannot meet while allowing Saudi Arabia to avoid explicitly rejecting Washington’s proposals. Riyadh can maintain that recognition remains possible, provided the occupying state meets its conditions.
A weakened Iran undermines the case for an alliance
For years, fear of Iran was the strongest argument for normalisation. An alliance with “Israel” was presented as a security necessity to deter Tehran and its proxies across the frontline states, rather than a choice driven by sentiment. Events since 2024 have overturned that calculation.
Successive strikes weakened Hezbollah’s military structure in Lebanon, depriving it of its longstanding leadership and much of its arsenal. The fall of the Assad regime in Syria severed the land corridor connecting Tehran to the Mediterranean. The subsequent US-Israeli war on Iran killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and dozens of military commanders, leaving the axis of resistance at its weakest in decades.
Iran’s response did reach Saudi territory. Riyadh condemned attacks on the Riyadh region and the Eastern Province, saying it had informed Tehran that it would not allow Saudi airspace or territory to be used to launch attacks against Iran. The war exposed the Gulf’s vulnerability to missiles and drones, but also showed that Iran could no longer dictate the course of events in the region. As the strategic threat from Iran receded, the strongest argument for a security alliance with “Israel” lost its force. Why should Riyadh pay the high price of normalisation to deter an adversary less capable of threatening it than before?
The kingdom used the resulting vacuum to expand its diplomatic influence, beginning with Syria. Since Assad’s fall, Riyadh has moved rapidly. It was the first capital President Ahmed al-Sharaa visited. Together with Doha, it paid Damascus’ arrears to the World Bank, then pressed Washington to lift sanctions until President Trump announced their removal during his visit to Riyadh. Economic agreements followed in energy, telecommunications and other sectors, including an agreement to establish a joint airline. Syria’s economy minister estimated Saudi investment in the country at more than $20 billion.
These commitments represent a political investment in a strategically sensitive country as well as economic support. After serving for two decades as Iran’s corridor to the Mediterranean, Syria could now strengthen the Arab states’ strategic position and permanently close that route to Tehran. It could also act as a barrier to Israeli encroachment in southern Syria, which Riyadh views as an attempt to establish new realities along the borders of a weakened Arab state. Saudi Arabia wants the new government in Damascus to become an active partner in the regional order it seeks to build, rather than leave Syria open to influence from Tehran, Tel Aviv or even its new ally, Ankara.
At the same time, Riyadh has maintained its commitment to the Beijing agreement with Tehran, at least in its public statements. About three months before the war, the Saudi-Iranian-Chinese trilateral committee met in Tehran to review implementation of the agreement. Even at the height of Iran’s attacks, Saudi statements continued to cite the deal and describe the assaults as a clear violation of it. Tehran, in turn, stressed that communication with Riyadh remained open and that it was still committed to the agreement.
Both countries need to preserve that commitment. A weakened Tehran wants to avoid facing another hostile front in the Gulf while fighting Washington and Tel Aviv. Riyadh wants a channel through which it can contain escalation, give China a role as guarantor in Gulf security and gain greater freedom to manoeuvre in its dealings with Washington and Tel Aviv. The Beijing agreement therefore provides a framework for managing their rivalry rather than ending it.
Saudi concerns over Israel’s military operations
While successive blows have forced Iran onto the defensive, “Israel” has emerged from its wars with a very different approach. It has acted as though its military power faces no limits, striking Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Iran. In September 2025, it extended its operations to Doha, targeting Hamas leaders in the heart of a Gulf capital allied with Washington. For Gulf capitals, the attack demonstrated that none was immune and that US guarantees could not prevent Israel from striking deep inside Arab countries.
Riyadh’s growing concern reflects its direct interests as well as political solidarity. Vision 2030 depends on stability, investment, tourism and the construction of new cities along the Red Sea coast. Every Israeli military operation that provokes an Iranian or Houthi response puts those projects at risk. The 2026 war demonstrated this when the Houthis announced the resumption of attacks in the Red Sea and imposed a blockade on Saudi tankers and ships. The kingdom found itself intercepting drones over its oil facilities during a war it had not chosen and had played no part in deciding to launch.
Another source of Saudi concern has received less attention. In December 2025, “Israel” officially recognised the breakaway region of “Somaliland,” alarming Riyadh. The move opened the way for increased military and intelligence activity.
Somali and European officials later reported that “Israel” had established an intelligence presence in Berbera. Other reports indicated that the region had provided Israel with a secret military site during the Iran war, allowing its aircraft to refuel on long-range missions. Authorities in Hargeisa repeatedly denied that an Israeli base existed. However, the region’s president openly expressed his desire to expand security cooperation in the future, amid reports of continuing military construction around Berbera airport.
Riyadh is further concerned that this activity is taking place on territory managed by the UAE, which is widely believed to have helped facilitate Israeli recognition. Here, Saudi concerns about “Israel” overlap with tensions with Abu Dhabi. Riyadh views Berbera as a staging point for operations, surveillance and intelligence: it overlooks the Gulf of Aden, commands the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and lies close to Saudi shores. The threat extends beyond maritime security to the East-West pipeline, which became Saudi Arabia’s most important oil export route during the Iran war, allowing it to bypass the closed Strait of Hormuz.
Riyadh responded in February 2026 by signing a military cooperation agreement with Somalia. articles.title: Trump Says Iran Deal Is Not His Preferred Option as Witkoff Pursues Talks - Khaama Press
articles.summary: Trump Says Iran Deal Is Not His Preferred Option as Witkoff Pursues Talks  Khaama Press
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that a potential agreement with Iran is not his preferred option, even as his special envoy, Steve Witkoff, continues diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the conflict.
Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Texas, Trump praised Witkoff’s work but signaled reluctance to pursue a formal deal with Tehran.
“He’s working on the Iran deal and doing very well,” Trump said, adding that an agreement was “really” not what he wanted but that Iran was willing to offer concessions to bring the conflict to an end.
Trump reiterated that Iran would never be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon and said he expected the war to end soon. He has repeatedly described U.S. military action as aimed at preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons.
The comments come as Washington and Tehran remain divided over the terms of a possible settlement. Recent U.S. proposals have focused on Iran’s nuclear activities, including uranium enrichment, while Tehran has sought sanctions relief, the release of frozen assets, an end to the naval blockade and arrangements for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Witkoff has previously taken part in mediated discussions with Iranian officials alongside Jared Kushner. Trump has described those talks as productive, while Iranian officials have expressed skepticism about negotiations amid continuing military pressure.
The latest remarks highlight the tension between Trump’s continued military pressure on Tehran and parallel diplomatic efforts to end the conflict. Trump has said the United States will remain focused on ensuring that Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon while seeking an end to the war.
The conflict, which began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28, has entered its eighth month, with the fighting also disrupting regional security and energy markets.

articles.title: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls - BBC
articles.summary: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls  BBCA year into Trump’s peace plan, Netanyahu stands in the way of rebuilding  The Washington PostIsrael’s ‘scorched-earth’ ceasefire in Gaza  Financial TimesIsrael kills or wounds Palestinian every 90 minutes in Gaza since ceasefire  Al Jazeera‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted.
"My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke.
He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in.
"Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said.
Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head.
She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
On the ground in Gaza, it meant that Israel's large-scale bombardment stopped, which brought substantial relief and an increase in humanitarian aid and medical supplies entering the territory.
But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. In the past week alone more than 30 people have been killed, according to Gaza's health ministry.
Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives, and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire.
"It [the ceasefire] is all lies. Every day there's a shooting. Every day there is killing and death lurking around," said Ahed, Fida's husband.
In response to the BBC's questions about Fida's killing, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they had no record of the incident.
The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza three years ago now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry.
Outside Fida's tent, her brother Ibrahim pointed to the holes he said were made by a volley of bullets fired by Israeli forces.
"This tent is just a piece of cloth. Imagine that a military vehicle came down here and fired a spray of bullets," he said. "There was also gunfire coming from the sky, from above, from quadcopters, and it was directed at unarmed civilians."
Fida is the fourth of Ibrahim's siblings to be killed since the start of the war. "We left our neighbourhood Zeitoun to survive, but death is following us," he said.
The family has moved seven times but safety has been out of reach. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced multiple times by the war, the UN says, with many forced to live in tented cities and unsafe structures.
On the same day that Fida was killed, 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil was also shot dead. He was killed in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, in southern Gaza.
His family told the BBC that he was shot by Israeli forces while he and his brothers were fishing in the Mediterranean Sea, around 20m (66ft) from the shore. He is one of more than 300 children killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to Gaza's health ministry.
The IDF said it had no information about this incident either.
Over the past year, the IDF has released videos of its operations in Gaza targeted at Hamas and other groups. At least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the start of the ceasefire.
Both Fida and Ismail lived close to the so-called Yellow Line that separates the areas occupied by the Israeli military in Gaza from areas controlled by Hamas in the west.
Areas around the line are considered the most dangerous because Israeli forces have frequently opened fire there. But there are few options to move because there is an extreme shortage of space.
The strip was densely populated even before the war began. Now, its population is squeezed into under 40% of its area, which is controlled by Hamas.
In those areas the group maintains a tight grip, clamping down on dissent and still recruiting fighters.
In May this year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had directed the IDF to increase the area of Gaza under Israel's control to 70%.
Architect Amal Alabadla, who lived in a comfortable flat prior to the war, now lives in a tent on the coastline.
"Every time the rains come, it gets flooded. I feel very scared when the wind is strong because our tent gets destroyed or damaged," she said.
Amal is forced to raise her two boys - Mohammed and Noah - on her own.
Her husband was not in Gaza when the war broke out, and in three years they have not been reunited. Amal's three brothers, who helped her care for the boys, were killed in separate attacks before the ceasefire began.
"During the winter, my son suffers from epilepsy seizures because of the cold. It's very hard sometimes to keep him dry and warm," she said.
"Before the war, I had a job, a house, an ordinary life, but then everything turned upside down. Now we have no hope, nothing. It's only about survival day by day, to keep my kids alive, clean, healthy and fed."
There are camps further inland in Gaza that have even been built below sea level, which are at greater risk of flooding.
The October 2025 peace deal was supposed to pave the way for the reconstruction in Gaza, but rebuilding has not yet begun - stuck in limbo because of an impasse over the second phase of the deal.
Israel strictly controls what materials and machinery are allowed into Gaza, acting, it says, for reasons of its own security.
Earlier this year, US President Donald Trump put forward a plan to disarm Hamas, but in August it was rejected by Netanyahu, who stated that no military pull-out would happen until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.
Hamas has said handing over its heavy weapons is contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.
Half a world away, Trump's Board of Peace has also proposed a recovery plan for Gaza worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn).
But, one year on from the ceasefire and three years on from the start of the war, many like Amal are deeply sceptical of things actually changing on the ground.
"We are struggling and not being allowed to rebuild," she said. "I don't think they are telling us the truth about allowing us to rebuild a safe future for our children."
Additional reporting by Imogen Anderson and Malak Hassouneh

articles.title: Gulf economies set for 10.3% rebound in 2027 if oil flows recover, says World Bank - https://internationalfinance.com/
articles.summary: Gulf economies set for 10.3% rebound in 2027 if oil flows recover, says World Bank  https://internationalfinance.com/
articles.full_text:
Gulf economies could stage a dramatic 10.3% rebound in 2027 if the conflict disrupting oil production and shipping subsides by the end of this year, the World Bank said, highlighting the region’s continued exposure to hydrocarbon flows even as governments accelerate diversification.
The forecast comes after an unusually severe shock to the Gulf Cooperation Council economies. The World Bank expects GCC output to contract by an average of 4.3% in 2026, with the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupting oil and gas exports, trade, tourism, aviation, and logistics.
The projected recovery is conditional on oil production and shipping returning to normal levels from early 2027. A restoration of hydrocarbon exports would provide the biggest immediate boost, while the return of tourism, trade, and domestic economic activity would broaden the recovery.
The World Bank said the wider Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan region is expected to contract 2.1% this year, following growth of 3.3% in 2025. If the conflict subsides by the end of 2026, growth across MENAAP excluding Iran could rebound to 7.8% in 2027, driven largely by the recovery in hydrocarbon production and exports.
The Gulf numbers, however, mask major differences between individual economies.
Qatar is expected to record the strongest expansion, with GDP forecast to grow 26.7% in 2027 as liquefied natural gas production resumes. Kuwait is projected to expand 22% as oil exports normalise, while the UAE is forecast to grow 9.5%.
Saudi Arabia, the region’s largest economy, is expected to contract 2% in 2026 before rebounding 7.9% next year. Bahrain and Oman are forecast to grow 4.2% and 3.4%, respectively.
The sharp variation indicates how disruptions to energy production and exports have impacted individual economies. For instance, Qatar’s forecast reflects the anticipated restart and ramp-up of LNG production, while Kuwait’s outlook closely ties to the restoration of oil shipments.
Saudi Arabia has been relatively better positioned than some of its neighbours because the East-West pipeline provides an alternative route for crude exports to Yanbu on the Red Sea, reducing its dependence on Hormuz.
The scale of the potential rebound is also a reminder that the Gulf’s diversification drive, while significant, has not removed the importance of hydrocarbons to economic growth.
The World Bank said the conflict has caused losses not only through reduced oil exports but also through weaker tourism, aviation, and logistics activity. Higher shipping costs have pushed up import prices, adding inflationary pressure across the region and straining supply chains.
Oil flows have already begun to recover, although they remain well below pre-conflict levels. Gulf exports excluding Iran averaged about 19.2 million barrels a day in September, or more than 81% of the pre-war level, according to Vortexa data reported by Reuters. Crude and condensate exports had recovered to about 91% of pre-war levels, while refined-fuel exports remained significantly weaker.
That distinction matters because restoring crude exports alone will not immediately resolve the disruption facing global energy markets. Damage to refineries and infrastructure has left refined products, particularly diesel and jet fuel, in much tighter supply.
The International Energy Agency has warned that the disruption could continue to weigh on the global oil supply until 2027. It expects the world oil supply to fall sharply in 2026, while demand is forecast to rebound in 2027 as energy markets stabilise.
For Gulf policymakers, the challenge will be converting a hydrocarbon-led rebound into more durable non-oil growth.
The IMF has similarly warned that the recovery depends on a gradual normalisation of shipping. It says GCC economies have shown resilience through fiscal and external buffers, strong banking systems, and investments in energy and logistics infrastructure.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE are particularly important to that diversification story. Construction, logistics, tourism, hospitality, financial services, and business services are expected to benefit as regional trade and investment recover.
The World Bank also sees artificial intelligence as a potential longer-term growth engine. It estimates that between 13% and 20% of jobs in the wider MENAAP region have significant potential to benefit from AI-driven productivity gains. Saudi Arabia and the UAE, with their growing computing capacity and investment in AI, are positioned to play a leading role.
Still, the 10.3% forecast should be viewed as a conditional recovery rather than a guaranteed boom. The World Bank cautioned that damaged infrastructure, postponed investment, and depleted fiscal buffers could continue to weigh on economies even after the immediate conflict ends.
For investors, the central question is therefore whether the 2027 rebound will simply reflect the restoration of oil production or become the beginning of a broader recovery in private investment and non-hydrocarbon activity.
If oil and shipping flows normalise, the Gulf could move from its sharpest downturn in years to one of its strongest expansions in a single year. But the sustainability of that rebound will ultimately depend on whether higher hydrocarbon revenues translate into productivity, private-sector investment, and deeper economic diversification.

articles.title: Rubio silent on claims US envoy to Greece sought $100K from donor
articles.summary: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio flatly refused to comment Thursday on a new report alleging that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle sought money from a donor and offe...
articles.full_text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio flatly refused to comment Thursday on a new report alleging that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle sought money from a donor and offered access to top administration officials.
Meanwhile, Vice President JD Vance said, "I don't love" the idea of a U.S. official asking someone to pay off debts in exchange for access to other government officials, but declined to comment further until he knew all the details.
"Of course, I don't like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official," Vance told reporters in Washington later Thursday. "I assume you're talking about a specific case, and I can't say with confidence that the case you're talking about is actually reflective of the way you're describing it."
During his trip to Greece, Rubio told reporters that he would not discuss the allegations contained in a Wall Street Journal story that said Guilfoyle had asked a donor and supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
He spoke before leaving Greece, where he delivered a speech calling for European countries to return to what he described as their civilizational roots.
Rubio said he was aware of WSJ's report, which was published late Wednesday, but had no idea if it was true and he would not address it.
"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," he said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart Greece, looked on.
At a joint news conference with the Greek foreign minister on Wednesday, Rubio said he would not address the allegations while visiting a foreign country, but added: "Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."
The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees have called for an investigation into Guilfoyle, but Rubio would not say if he was prepared to open one.
Congressional Democrats already were looking into claims reported last month by the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle acted improperly while serving as the top U.S. envoy to Greece.
The Journal reported that Guilfoyle told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump's son Donald Jr., has denied any wrongdoing and Rubio has defended her before.

articles.summary: NATO announced plans to begin its annual nuclear deterrence exercises in Italy on Tuesday, as growing concerns over Russia heighten security tensions across Europe. Its "Steadfast...
articles.full_text:
NATO announced plans to begin its annual nuclear deterrence exercises in Italy on Tuesday, as growing concerns over Russia heighten security tensions across Europe.
Its "Steadfast Noon" drills will run from Oct. 13 to 23 and will involve 17 nations, it said Thursday.
"The exercise is a long-planned, routine training activity that is part of NATO's efforts to maintain readiness and test procedures that contribute to the alliance's deterrence and defence," said a NATO statement.
"No live weapons are used in Steadfast Noon. The exercise is not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country," the alliance added.
But NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte commented that while NATO was a "defensive alliance" the exercise "helps us ensure a safe, secure, effective, and credible capability to preserve peace, prevent coercion and deter aggression. It also sends a clear message of unity and resolve".
Russia, embroiled in an invasion of Ukraine since 2022, has accused NATO of staging "provocative" actions around its exclave of Kaliningrad.
It has warned that it is ready to use "its entire arsenal."
NATO condemned the comments, but its officials say the alliance has not seen major changes in Russia's nuclear posture.

articles.title: Russia boosts prewinter strikes, killing 33 in Ukraine's Kramatorsk
articles.summary: Russian strikes in eastern Ukraine killed at least 33 people and injured some 18 on Thursday, striking a public bus as worsening power outages hit Kyiv amid an escalating prewinter...
articles.full_text:
Russian strikes in eastern Ukraine killed at least 33 people and injured some 18 on Thursday, striking a public bus as worsening power outages hit Kyiv amid an escalating prewinter campaign.
Vadym Filashkin, head of the regional military administration, said public transport in Kramatorsk and the neighboring city of Sloviansk, in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, was halted because of the sharp deterioration in security.
He accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians, adding: "For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target, precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible," Filashkin said.
"Russia is deliberately flouting every conceivable rule of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest harm on the civilian population," he added.
"In such circumstances, we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers. The safety of residents of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is above all," said Filashkin.
The Kramatorsk City Council called it "yet another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population."
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it added.
The attacks follow deadly missile strikes a day earlier in the northern Ukrainian town of Pryluky, where the death toll rose to 22, including five children.
Rescuers searched through the rubble of a residential building hit by a Russian missile and at least 54 people were injured.
Heavy debris was removed from the cratered section of the building, while rescue dogs continued a search nearby for residents who have not yet been accounted for.
Several survivors of the attack were forced to sleep in heavily damaged apartments after they couldn't find anywhere else to sleep.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Russia will likely escalate daily missile and drone attacks as winter approaches. He appealed for additional defense support from NATO countries.
"It is important that support in words takes concrete form in new packages for Ukraine's defense," he wrote in an online post.
"Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors – all of this is directly helping save lives every day," he added.
Ukraine's energy company DTEK said the national grid operator Ukrenergo had ordered emergency power outages in Kyiv. It explained that this is separate from regular, rolling outages scheduled across the country and would not be applied during those shutdowns.
A public awareness campaign, restarted this month, urged families to prepare emergency kits, store drinking water and maintain off-grid power sources ahead of expected prolonged winter blackouts, as Moscow keeps up the intensity of its attacks.
Kyiv police said bomb disposal specialists had defused two more unexploded ballistic missile warheads, each weighing about half a ton, after they landed near residential buildings.
Late Wednesday, Russian drones struck Kyiv’s Obolonskyi and Desnianskyi districts, killing four people and injuring 12, including four children, police said.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
Russia’s technology giant Yandex said one of its data centers in the western Ryazan region was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack, taking the site offline and leading to potential online service disruption.
Separately, Ukraine said its forces struck a large oil refinery complex in the city of Salavat, some 1,200 kilometers (about 750 miles) east of Moscow.
Ukraine's General Staff described the complex as one of Russia’s largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities. The claim could not be independently verified.

articles.title: French youth ignores PM pledge to continue school blockades
articles.summary: Students in France continued their blockade of high schools and marched through cities Thursday after the government offered no details on promised remedies for teacher shortages a...
articles.full_text:
Students in France continued their blockade of high schools and marched through cities Thursday after the government offered no details on promised remedies for teacher shortages and dilapidated facilities.
The protest movement, now into its third week, has exposed deep tensions in France between popular demands for investments in deteriorating public services and a cash-strapped government under pressure from bond markets to reduce its debt and deficit.
It has also led to thousands of arrests, dozens of injuries and a heated debate about the use of force by riot police against teenagers. On Wednesday, the government suspended the use of stun grenades in the policing of the protests.
The Education Ministry said 224 high schools were closed Thursday morning, while 151 were partially reopening after closures. It said the number of closures had dropped by 30% compared with Wednesday morning and that 94% of high schools were either fully or partially open.
Live footage on TV channels showed marches were again under way Thursday in Nantes, Rennes, Bron, Toulon and Marseille, two days after hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets nationwide. An afternoon rally was planned on Place de la Bastille in Paris.
Near Helene Boucher high school in the 20th arrondissement of Paris, a predominantly working-class area, a barricade formed out of rubbish bins had been erected and protesters chanted and held up banners. Scuffles with police broke out.
Charlotte Beaubeau, an English teacher, said she was at the blockade to show solidarity with the students and described the police response to the wave of protests as heavy-handed.
"There are a number of adults making sure that everything is okay for them," she said.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu addressed the nation late Wednesday, pledging that the government would present "concrete, quick and fully funded responses" by late October, without offering specifics.
An online consultation platform set up for high-school students to express their frustrations and make their demands had drawn more than 43,000 responses in its first two days.
But the government is under pressure from a range of sectors demanding support, even as its borrowing costs have surged due to market concerns about strained public finances.
On Thursday morning, the Agriculture Ministry announced 2 billion euros ($2.24 billion) in interest-free loans for farmers, in addition to a 1.3 billion euros emergency aid package announced last month after this summer's record heat waves and droughts.
Six months out from an election to replace President Emmanuel Macron after the end of his second consecutive term, politicians' responses to the wave of student protests have been starkly polarized.
Far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen has highlighted damage to schools caused by a minority of protesters and called for them or their parents to foot repair bills. On Tuesday, she outlined plans to slash public spending should she win.
Her hard-left opponent Jean-Luc Melenchon, who also has a chance of making the runoff, has praised the protesters as "incredible" and denounced police brutality.
According to an Elabe poll for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students' demands are legitimate, but 55% of them think the protests should stop.
The government has sought to tread a line between condemning violent incidents in which schools were set ablaze and staff injured, while also expressing sympathy with some of the students' complaints.
In Belgium, protests were taking place outside some schools in Brussels and outside Liege University, broadcaster RTBF reported.
In Liege, where local media have reported more than 100 arrests in connection with student protests this month, authorities have imposed a ban on public gatherings of more than three people until Oct. 16. However, police said the university protest had been authorized.
Belgium's Foreign Minister Bernard Quintin said hard-left activists had infiltrated the Liege school protests and were causing damage to property.
Julien Doeche, a member of the Liege Antifascist Front, told RTBF Quintin's claims were "fantasies."

articles.summary: Ethiopian drone strikes targeted Eritrean forces inside a northern Tigrayan city on Thursday, conflict monitors and witnesses said, raising fears of a broader regional war. Relatio...

Ethiopian drone strikes targeted Eritrean forces inside a northern Tigrayan city on Thursday, conflict monitors and witnesses said, raising fears of a broader regional war.
Relations between the two neighboring countries, who fought a brutal border war between 1998-2000, have sharply deteriorated recently.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing rebels in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region and the two countries severed diplomatic ties last week.
On Wednesday, sources said Eritrean troops had crossed the border and were positioned around the city of Adigrat.
Conflict monitor ACLED said that "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in the Adigrat area were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight.
"There were many, many drone strikes yesterday, some Eritrean lorries have been destroyed, they are no more in the streets," one witness, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told AFP.
Neither Asmara nor Addis Ababa have yet responded to inquiries about the situation in northern Ethiopia.
The allegations come amid renewed fighting between Ethiopian government forces and an opposition alliance that includes the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accused Ethiopia on Wednesday of fabricating allegations to justify military action against his country.
In a post on X, he accused Ethiopia’s ruling party of creating "a fallacious narrative of ‘self-defense.’” He did not specifically address the movements or strikes described by ACLED.
Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia during the 2020-2022 civil war against the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
But the relationship soon deteriorated, particularly over landlocked Ethiopia's persistent claims that it has a right to sea access.

articles.title: Malaysia promises Myanmar help toward full ASEAN reintegration
articles.summary: Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Thursday his government would do "whatever possible" to reintegrate Myanmar into ASEAN following a meeting with the country's leader, Mi...
articles.full_text:
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Thursday his government would do "whatever possible" to reintegrate Myanmar into ASEAN following a meeting with the country's leader, Min Aung Hlaing.
Anwar also pledged to continue working with Myanmar, including on the repatriation of thousands of Myanmar nationals from Malaysia – a move the United Nations and rights groups have widely criticized, citing risks from an ongoing civil war.
Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing is on a two-day visit to Malaysia as he seeks greater international legitimacy after becoming president in April following an election that Western nations and rights groups widely criticized as a sham.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since 2021 when Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup against a democratically elected government, triggering armed conflict across much of the country.
Min Aung Hlaing and other senior Myanmar officials have been barred from attending ASEAN summits after failing to adhere to an ASEAN-brokered peace plan following the coup, but some member countries have sought to reestablish ties.
Since becoming president, Min Aung Hlaing has also visited ASEAN members Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam.
Malaysia's Anwar acknowledged ongoing concerns about democratic processes in Myanmar but said differences should be respected, adding Min Aung Hlaing had shown a willingness to collaborate.
"We in Malaysia will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration and, ultimately, take Myanmar as part of our community of nations, without prejudice and particularly in the context of ASEAN," Anwar told a news conference following the meeting.
Anwar also expressed appreciation to Min Aung Hlaing for accepting the repatriation of 10,493 Myanmar nationals from Malaysia so far.
Malaysia has said it can no longer take in refugees from Myanmar, saying they had become a financial burden and a security risk. Malaysia is not a party to the United Nations refugee convention and treats asylum-seekers as illegal migrants.
The country last month sent back around 1,500 people on Myanmar naval ships, part of a wider repatriation program that could see as many as 5,000 people deported.
Min Aung Hlaing said at Thursday's news conference Myanmar citizens currently held at Malaysian immigration detention centers would be brought back as soon as possible.
"Because the current weather is favorable, I will send navy ships to repatriate them," he said, adding he would formally request Malaysia allow the repatriation.
He also extended an invitation for Anwar to visit Myanmar "when the time is right."
Anwar and Min Aung Hlaing did not mention if their discussions included plans to repatriate Rohingya Muslim refugees, many of whom fled Myanmar after a brutal 2017 military crackdown in the country's Rakhine state that is now the subject of a genocide case at the International Court of Justice.
Muslim-majority Malaysia widely criticized the crackdown at the time.
But public sentiment has turned in recent years, with the Rohingya in Malaysia facing increasing harassment and scrutiny amid a surge of online hate speech and misinformation. Anwar has said he would push for Myanmar to accept Rohingya refugees.
There are more than 193,000 refugees and asylum-seekers from Myanmar in Malaysia, about 65% of them Rohingya, according to the United Nations refugee agency.
Buddhist-majority Myanmar does not recognize the Rohingya as one of its official ethnic groups and denies citizenship to most.
